metadata.title: ELITE Step 2 CK Orthopaedic Q-Bank
metadata.description: Multiple-choice questions organized by topics and chapters.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman with a history of a cerebrovascular accident (CVA) presenting with residual left-sided hemiparesis is observed during an outpatient physical therapy evaluation. During the swing phase of walking, she noticeably abducts her paretic left lower extremity and swings it forward in a wide semicircular outward motion to prevent the toes from scuffing or clearing the floor. She also demonstrates internal rotation and plantarflexion of the left foot. Which of the following gait patterns is demonstrated?
questions.explanation:
This patient demonstrates a classic circumductory hemiplegic gait (also known as a spastic hemiplegic gait). Following an upper motor neuron (UMN) injury such as an ischemic stroke or hemorrhagic CVA, patients develop spastic hemiparesis characterized by increased extensor tone in the lower extremity and flexor hypertonia in the upper extremity. In the lower extremity, hypertonia of the quadriceps and gastrocnemius-soleus complex causes loss of voluntary knee flexion, ankle dorsiflexion weakness, and equinovarus posturing (foot drop). Because the paretic leg is functionally 'too long' during the swing phase, the patient must hike the pelvis (hip hiking) and swing the leg outward in a lateral semicircle (circumduction) to advance the limb without the toes dragging along the floor.

High-yield clinical pearl: UPPER MOTOR NEURON SPASTIC HEMIPLEGIA:
Lower extremity extensor synergy (hip extension/adduction, knee extension, ankle plantarflexion/inversion) leads to a functional leg length discrepancy, compensated by hip hiking and outward circumduction during the swing phase.

Exam trap: Do not confuse HIGH STEPPAGE GAIT (L5/deep fibular nerve flaccid foot drop requiring exaggerated hip/knee flexion) with CIRCUMDUCTORY GAIT (UMN spasticity where the knee cannot easily flex, forcing lateral outward swinging).

optionExplanations.A: Trendelenburg gait is caused by abductor mechanism deficiency (gluteus medius/minimus weakness or superior gluteal nerve lesion). The pelvis drops toward the contralateral, unsupported swing side during single-leg stance.
optionExplanations.B: Shuffling gait (festinating gait) is characteristic of Parkinson's disease and basal ganglia pathology, marked by short, flat-footed, hurried steps with reduced arm swing and stooped posture.
optionExplanations.C: Spastic hemiparesis after an upper motor neuron lesion (stroke) leaves the paretic leg functionally too long and stiff at the knee, so the patient hikes the pelvis and swings the leg outward in a wide arc (circumduction) to clear the floor.
optionExplanations.D: High steppage gait results from isolated foot drop secondary to common fibular (peroneal) nerve injury or L5 radiculopathy; the patient excessively flexes the hip and knee to lift the flaccid foot off the floor without circumduction.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that spastic hemiplegia from a cerebrovascular accident creates an excessively extended, stiff lower limb that requires a circumductory gait pattern to ensure ground clearance during the swing phase.

questions.question: A clinician performs the physical examination shown in the clinical photograph. The patient is placed in the supine position on the examination table. The examiner places one hand beneath the lumbar spine and maximally flexes the contralateral hip until the lumbar lordosis is flattened against the hand. The examiner then observes the behavior of the test hip (the extended hip remaining on the table). Which one of the following statements is true regarding this maneuver and its findings?

options.A: The test is primarily used to assess PCL rupture in the knee
options.B: The patient has weakness of the right hip abductors due to superior gluteal nerve injury
options.C: The findings are most consistent with rupture of the right tendon Achilles
options.D: The examiner places his hand beneath the lumbar spine to ensure persistence of lumbar lordosis during hip flexion
options.E: Right hip fixed flexion, the left hip is normal

questions.explanation:
The maneuver depicted is the Thomas test, the cardinal clinical examination for identifying and quantifying a fixed flexion contracture of the hip (frequently seen in osteoarthritis, psoas muscle abscess/contracture, or spasticity). Under normal conditions, a patient can easily mask a hip flexion contracture while standing or supine by exaggerating their lumbar lordosis (anterior pelvic tilt). To accurately unmask the true deformity, the examiner places a hand beneath the lumbar spine to monitor the lumbar curvature. As the contralateral hip and knee are brought into maximal flexion toward the chest, the pelvis rotates posteriorly, flattening the lumbar lordosis firmly against the examiner's hand. If a fixed flexion deformity exists on the test side, the ipsilateral thigh involuntarily lifts off the examination surface. The angle between the elevated thigh and the examination table corresponds directly to the degree of fixed flexion deformity.

High-yield clinical pearl: THOMAS TEST MECHANICS:
Unmasks occult hip flexion deformity by neutralizing compensatory lumbar lordosis. Flexing the unaffected hip rotates the pelvis posteriorly; an unable-to-extend ipsilateral thigh confirms psoas/capsular contracture.

Exam trap: In the exam key, pay careful attention to the examiner's hand placement: placing the hand under the lumbar spine ensures the clinician verifies whether lumbar lordosis is being actively eliminated or controlled during contralateral flexion.

optionExplanations.A: Assessment of PCL rupture is performed using the posterior drawer test, posterior sag sign (Godfrey test), or quadriceps active test, not the Thomas test.
optionExplanations.B: Weakness of the hip abductors is evaluated using the Trendelenburg test in single-leg stance.
optionExplanations.C: Achilles tendon rupture is diagnosed clinically using the Thompson (Simmonds) calf-squeeze test.
optionExplanations.D: Marked correct in the source key. In the Thomas test the examiner's hand beneath the lumbar spine is used to monitor the lumbar curve while the contralateral hip is flexed. REVIEW FLAG: this option says the hand ensures 'persistence' of lordosis, but the stem and the source rationale describe lordosis being flattened against the hand, and option E (right hip fixed flexion) appears to be the clinically valid statement; see extraction_report.txt.
optionExplanations.E: The description refers to the technique of the test itself; the examiner monitors the lumbar spine to detect pelvic rotation and eliminate lordosis compensation.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand the biomechanical principle of the Thomas test: maximal flexion of the contralateral hip flattens the lumbar spine, preventing compensatory lordosis and unmasking true fixed flexion contracture of the hip.

questions.question: A pediatric orthopedic surgeon examines two young children with lower extremity angular variations, designated Patient A and Patient B as shown in the accompanying clinical photographs. Patient A demonstrates an increased intercondylar distance with knees curved outward away from the midline. Patient B demonstrates touching medial femoral condyles with an abnormally widened intermalleolar distance between the medial malleoli. Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the deformities seen in patients A and B?

options.A: Both deformities are in coronal plane
options.B: Patient A has knee valgus, while patient B has knee varus
options.D: Both deformities represent sagittal plane malalignments

questions.explanation:
Angular deformities of the extremities are classified according to the anatomical plane in which the deviation occurs: Coronal (frontal) plane deformities represent medial or lateral angular deviations, namely varus (apex pointing laterally, distal segment directed medially) and valgus (apex pointing medially, distal segment directed laterally). Patient A exhibits genu varum (bow-legs), where the tibia is deviated medially relative to the femur in the coronal plane, producing a widened intercondylar distance. Patient B exhibits genu valgum (knock-knees), where the distal leg is deviated laterally relative to the femur in the coronal plane, producing a widened intermalleolar distance. Because both varus and valgus represent angulations seen on an anteroposterior projection, both deformities reside strictly within the coronal plane.

High-yield clinical pearl: NORMAL PEDIATRIC CORONAL ALIGNMENT EVOLUTION:
• Birth to 18–24 months: Physiologic Genu Varum (up to 15°).
• 2 to 4 years: Neutral transitions into maximal Physiologic Genu Valgum (up to 10–12°).
• By age 7 years: Stabilizes to adult normal valgus (~5–7°).

Exam trap: Remember anatomical planes: CORONAL = VARUS/VALGUS; SAGITTAL = FLEXION/EXTENSION/RECURVATUM; TRANSVERSE = ANTEVERSION/RETROVERSION/INTERNAL-EXTERNAL ROTATION.

optionExplanations.A: Genu varum (Patient A) and genu valgum (Patient B) are both medial/lateral angular deviations, which are coronal (frontal) plane deformities.
optionExplanations.B: This statement reverses the clinical diagnoses; Patient A has knee varus (bowing out) and Patient B has knee valgus (knees touch).
optionExplanations.C: Translation represents a translational shift (displacement) along an axis, whereas varus and valgus are angular deformities.
optionExplanations.D: Sagittal plane deformities of the knee comprise flexion contractures and hyperextension deformities (genu recurvatum), not varus or valgus.

questions.educationalObjective: Classify lower extremity angular alignments accurately, recognizing that genu varum and genu valgum are angular deformities occurring strictly in the coronal (frontal) plane.

questions.question: A patient is evaluated for hip instability. When asked to stand on one foot, the clinician observes the pelvic kinematics shown in the illustration. During single-leg stance on the affected limb, the contralateral pelvis drops downwards below the horizontal plane instead of being elevated. Regarding this picture, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Left superior gluteal nerve injury with ischemia
options.C: Hip will tilt to the right side

questions.explanation:
The Trendelenburg test assesses the integrity of the hip abductor mechanism (gluteus medius and minimus muscles innervated by the superior gluteal nerve, L4–S1). When standing on one leg, the abductor muscles of the weight-bearing (stance) limb must contract powerfully to prevent the unsupported opposite side of the pelvis from dropping due to gravity. If the abductor mechanism on the stance side is compromised (due to superior gluteal nerve palsy, severe hip osteoarthritis, developmental dysplasia, or L5 radiculopathy), the abductors cannot stabilize the pelvis. Consequently, the pelvis tilts (drops) downward toward the contralateral, unsupported swing side. In this clinical scenario and question key, standing on the affected stance leg causes the hip/pelvis to tilt downward toward the opposite (right) side.

High-yield clinical pearl: TRENDELENBURG SIGN RULE:
• The defective abductor is on the STANCE (WEIGHT-BEARING) LEG.
• The pelvic drop is on the CONTRALATERAL (SWING/UNSUPPORTED) SIDE.
• Trendelenburg lurch (gait): The patient leans their torso over the stance leg to shift the center of gravity over the hip fulcrum.

Exam trap: Board questions constantly test the direction of drop: pathology on the Left stance hip = pelvic drop on the Right swing hip.

optionExplanations.A: The gluteus medius and minimus are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve, but isolated ischemia is exceedingly rare; the typical etiologies are nerve traction/laceration during hip arthroplasty (lateral Hardinge approach) or pelvic fracture.
optionExplanations.B: Weakness on the stance side causes pelvic drop on the contralateral side; if the pelvis drops to the right, the pathology is in the left hip abductors.
optionExplanations.C: Marked correct in the source key. When the stance-side hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus) fail, the pelvis drops toward the opposite, unsupported side; the source rationale states the pelvis tilts down to the right in this scenario. REVIEW FLAG: the stem does not say which side is affected, and option A (left superior gluteal nerve injury) is also consistent with a right-sided drop; see extraction_report.txt.
optionExplanations.D: The sciatic nerve innervates the hamstring muscles and gives rise to the tibial and common fibular nerves; it does not innervate the hip abductors.

questions.educationalObjective: Master the biomechanics of the Trendelenburg sign: abductor deficiency on the stance side causes the pelvis to tilt/drop down on the contralateral unsupported side.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with a 12-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with progressive, worsening right shoulder pain and stiffness over the past 6 months. She reports profound difficulty reaching behind her back to fasten her bra and combing her hair. On physical examination, there is marked, symmetrical restriction of both active and passive range of motion in all planes, particularly external rotation and abduction. Forward elevation is limited to 80° and external rotation is limited to 15°. Plain radiographs of the glenohumeral joint demonstrate normal articular cartilage space without osteophytes or fractures. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.E: Corticosteroid and physical therapy

questions.explanation:
This patient presents with classic adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder), a condition characterized by progressive glenohumeral capsular fibrosis, thickening, and contracture. Adhesive capsulitis is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus (present in up to 20% of diabetic patients), hypothyroidism, and prolonged immobilization. The hallmark physical examination finding that distinguishes adhesive capsulitis from rotator cuff tear or subacromial impingement is an equal limitation of BOTH active and passive range of motion, particularly in external rotation and abduction. First-line management is conservative: structured physical therapy (gentle stretching and range-of-motion exercises) combined with anti-inflammatory analgesics and/or an intra-articular glenohumeral corticosteroid injection to alleviate pain and accelerate functional recovery. Surgical intervention (manipulation under anesthesia or arthroscopic capsular release) is strictly reserved for refractory cases failing at least 6 to 12 months of intensive non-operative therapy.

High-yield clinical pearl: ADHESIVE CAPSULITIS CLINICAL TRIAD:
1. Equal restriction of active AND passive glenohumeral motion (external rotation affected earliest).
2. Strong association with Diabetes Mellitus and Thyroid disease.
3. Normal plain radiographs (rules out glenohumeral osteoarthritis).

Exam trap: If passive range of motion is normal while active motion is restricted/painful, suspect ROTATOR CUFF PATHOLOGY (tear or tendinopathy). When both active and passive motion are restricted, it is ADHESIVE CAPSULITIS or advanced glenohumeral osteoarthritis.

optionExplanations.A: Sling immobilization is absolutely contraindicated; immobilization promotes further capsular fibrosis, worsening joint stiffness.
optionExplanations.B: Arthroscopic debridement and capsular release are second-line operative interventions indicated only after prolonged failed conservative therapy.
optionExplanations.C: Open surgical release has high morbidity and is rarely performed in the modern arthroscopic era.
optionExplanations.D: Manipulation under anesthesia carries risks of humeral shaft fracture, glenoid labral tear, or brachial plexus traction injury; it is not first-line.
optionExplanations.E: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder), with equal loss of active and passive motion in a diabetic patient, is treated first-line conservatively with corticosteroid injection plus physical therapy.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify adhesive capsulitis by its pathognomonic equal reduction in active and passive glenohumeral range of motion and recognize corticosteroid injection plus physical therapy as first-line therapy.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with a 15-year history of severe, seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is scheduled for elective total knee arthroplasty under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation. Preoperative cervical spine flexion-extension radiographs are ordered to evaluate the cervical spine. Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE regarding cervical spine involvement in this patient?

options.A: Atlantoaxial instability is not related to down syndrome
options.B: Atlantoaxial instability is clinically important only after cervical trauma
options.C: The atlantoaxial joint is a saddle synovial joint
options.D: Neck manipulation during intubation may precipitate spinal cord or medullary injury

questions.explanation:
Patients with longstanding, active rheumatoid arthritis (RA) develop progressive synovial inflammation (pannus) within the synovial bursa surrounding the odontoid process (dens) of C2. This chronic proliferative synovitis leads to laxity, erosion, and eventual rupture of the transverse ligament of the atlas, producing atlantoaxial subluxation (instability) in up to 30–50% of chronic RA patients. During endotracheal intubation, direct laryngoscopy requires cervical extension and atlantoaxial manipulation. In patients with unstable C1–C2 subluxation, forceful neck manipulation or excessive flexion/extension can cause the dens to displace posteriorly into the spinal canal, leading to catastrophic cervical spinal cord contusion, quadriplegia, or fatal medullary compression with respiratory arrest. Therefore, routine preoperative cervical flexion-extension radiographs are mandatory prior to elective intubation in chronic RA patients, and fiberoptic video-assisted intubation without neck manipulation is utilized when instability is documented.

High-yield clinical pearl: ANTERIOR ATLANTOAXIAL SUBLUXATION MEASUREMENT:
Diagnosed on lateral cervical flexion radiograph when the ANTERIOR ATLANTO-DENS INTERVAL (ADI) exceeds 3 MM IN ADULTS (or >5 mm in children). An ADI >9–10 mm indicates high risk for cord compression and warrants neurosurgical/orthopedic stabilization.

Exam trap: Never intubate an RA patient requiring general anesthesia without first confirming cervical spine clearance or utilizing video-guided in-line stabilization.

optionExplanations.A: Atlantoaxial instability is very strongly associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) due to generalized ligamentous laxity and hypoplasia of the dens.
optionExplanations.B: Atlantoaxial instability in RA develops insidiously and spontaneously from chronic inflammatory pannus erosion without preceding trauma.
optionExplanations.C: The median atlantoaxial joint is a trochoid (pivot) synovial joint, and the lateral atlantoaxial joints are plane synovial joints; neither is a saddle joint.
optionExplanations.D: In long-standing RA, pannus can rupture the transverse ligament and cause atlantoaxial subluxation; forceful neck flexion or extension during intubation can then displace the dens posteriorly and injure the spinal cord or medulla.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that chronic rheumatoid arthritis causes pannus destruction of the transverse ligament at C1–C2, creating atlantoaxial instability that poses a life-threatening risk of spinal cord or medullary injury during airway manipulation.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with persistent, bilateral knee pain, marked warmth, and morning stiffness lasting more than 90 minutes. She also reports recurrent episodes of bilateral episcleritis and symmetrical swelling of her wrists and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints. Physical examination demonstrates large, warm, boggy bilateral knee effusions with symmetrical joint line tenderness. Plain weight-bearing anteroposterior radiographs of the knees are obtained. Which of the following radiographic patterns is most consistent with her underlying disease?

options.A: Isolated asymmetric medial compartment joint space narrowing with heavy subchondral sclerosis
options.B: Prominent marginal osteophyte formation with preserved lateral joint space
options.C: Uniform, symmetrical tricompartmental joint space narrowing with periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions
options.D: Subchondral cyst formation confined strictly to the weight-bearing femoral condyle with dense sclerosis
options.E: Complete preservation of cartilage space with cortical hyperostosis

questions.explanation:
This young woman presents with textbook features of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA): symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour), and systemic extra-articular manifestations (episcleritis). In rheumatoid arthritis, the primary pathology is chronic proliferative synovitis (pannus formation). Because the entire synovial lining is inflamed, cartilage destruction occurs globally across the whole joint. Consequently, the pathognomonic radiographic features of RA include: 1. Uniform, symmetrical loss of joint space (affecting both medial and lateral compartments equally). 2. Periarticular osteopenia (due to inflammatory hyperemia and localized cytokine-mediated osteoclast activation). 3. Marginal bone erosions at the 'bare areas' where bone is not protected by articular cartilage. 4. Absence of reactive bone formation (osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis are notably absent in pure RA).

High-yield clinical pearl: RADIOLOGY MNEMONIC (OA VS RA):
• OA = LOSS:
Loss of joint space (asymmetric), Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts.
• RA = POSE:
Periarticular Osteopenia, Symmetric joint narrowing, Erosions (marginal).

Exam trap: Symmetric tricompartmental narrowing points to inflammatory arthritis (RA), whereas asymmetric unicompartmental narrowing (typically medial knee) indicates mechanical wear (OA).

optionExplanations.A: Asymmetric joint space narrowing with heavy subchondral sclerosis is the cardinal hallmark of osteoarthritis (Image B/D).
optionExplanations.B: Osteophyte formation is a reparative bone process characteristic of osteoarthritis, not rheumatoid arthritis.
optionExplanations.C: RA destroys the whole joint through pannus-mediated synovitis, giving uniform symmetric tricompartmental joint-space loss, periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions, without osteophytes or sclerosis.
optionExplanations.D: Subchondral cysts with dense sclerosis localized to one condyle represent advanced osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.E: Preservation of joint space is inconsistent with symptomatic, chronic inflammatory destructive synovitis.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish the radiographic features of rheumatoid arthritis (uniform symmetric cartilage loss, periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions) from osteoarthritis (asymmetric joint narrowing, osteophytes, eburnation).

questions.question: A plain lateral radiograph of a normal adult elbow joint is reviewed. Which of the following statements regarding the functional anatomy and stability of the elbow joint is CORRECT?

options.A: The capitulum articulates with the coronoid process
options.B: Pulled elbow in children is considered a complex elbow dislocation
options.C: The main stabilizers in this joint are the collateral ligaments
options.D: The elbow joint is a saddle synovial joint

questions.explanation:
The elbow joint is an inherently stable ginglymus (hinge) synovial joint allowing flexion and extension, coupled with a trochoidea (pivot) joint allowing forearm pronation and supination. Biomechanical stability of the elbow is divided into primary and secondary stabilizers: 1. Primary static stabilizers: The ulnohumeral articulation (bony congruity of the olecranon and coronoid process within the humeral trochlea), the anterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament (MCL) (primary restraint to valgus stress), and the lateral collateral ligament complex (specifically the LUCL) (primary restraint to varus and posterolateral rotatory instability). 2. Secondary stabilizers: The radial head articulating with the capitulum, the anterior joint capsule, and the dynamic common flexor/extensor muscle tendons. Therefore, the collateral ligaments and ulnohumeral congruity are the fundamental primary stabilizers of the elbow.

High-yield clinical pearl: PRIMARY ELBOW VALGUS RESTRAINT:
The ANTERIOR BUNDLE OF THE MEDIAL COLLATERAL LIGAMENT (MCL) is the single most important restraint to valgus stress across 20° to 120° of elbow flexion (injured in overhead throwing athletes requiring Tommy John reconstruction).

Exam trap: Remember: The RADIAL HEAD articulates with the CAPITULUM (C-R: Capitulum with Radius), while the TROCHLEA articulates with the ULNA.

optionExplanations.A: The capitulum articulates with the radial head (radiocapitellar joint). The coronoid process articulates with the coronoid fossa of the humerus above the trochlea.
optionExplanations.B: Pulled elbow (nursemaid's elbow) in toddlers is an isolated subluxation of the annular ligament over the radial head without complex capsular or ligamentous disruption.
optionExplanations.C: The collateral ligaments (anterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament and the lateral ulnar collateral ligament complex), together with ulnohumeral bony congruity, are the primary static stabilizers of the elbow.
optionExplanations.D: The elbow is a hinge (ginglymus) joint; the thumb carpometacarpal (CMC) joint is the classic saddle (sellar) synovial joint.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall elbow joint functional anatomy: it is a hinge joint whose primary static stability is provided by the collateral ligaments and ulnohumeral articular congruity.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman with severe, end-stage rheumatoid arthritis demonstrates advanced bilateral hand deformities as shown in the clinical photograph. Both hands exhibit extensive metacarpophalangeal (MCP) subluxation, ulnar deviation (drift) of the digits, and marked finger deformities. Careful examination of the individual digits reveals characteristic tendon imbalance patterns. In this rheumatoid patient, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: Swan neck deformity is seen in the right thumb
options.B: Index finger of both hands has boutonniere's deformity
options.C: No ulnar deviation is seen at MCP joints in both hands
options.D: The little finger of the left hand has boutonniere's deformity

questions.explanation:
Chronic rheumatoid synovitis within the flexor tendon sheaths and interphalangeal joints destroys the delicate extensor mechanism balance of the fingers: 1. Boutonnière deformity: Caused by rupture or attenuation of the central slip of the extensor tendon over the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, allowing the lateral bands to subluxate volarly below the axis of motion. This produces PIP joint flexion with reciprocal distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint hyperextension. In this patient, the little finger of the left hand clearly displays this fixed flexion at the PIP joint and extension at the DIP joint. 2. Swan neck deformity: Caused by laxity or stretching of the volar plate at the PIP joint, resulting in PIP joint hyperextension with reciprocal DIP joint flexion (resembling a swan's neck). 3. Ulnar drift: Severe ulnar deviation of digits 2 through 5 at the MCP joints due to attenuation of radial collateral ligaments and extensor digitorum communis tendon subluxation into the ulnar valleys.

High-yield clinical pearl: MNEMONIC FOR HAND DEFORMITIES:
• BOUTONNIÈRE:
Buttonhole = Flexion of PIP, Extension of DIP.
• SWAN NECK:
Swan flies high = Hyperextension of PIP, Flexion of DIP.

Exam trap: Do not confuse the joint levels! Boutonniere = PIP Flexion / DIP Extension. Swan Neck = PIP Extension / DIP Flexion.

optionExplanations.A: The rheumatoid thumb typically develops either a Boutonnière-like deformity (Z-deformity: MCP flexion with IP hyperextension) or a Swan neck-like deformity (CMC subluxation, MCP hyperextension, IP flexion); Option A is factually incorrect on the clinical image.
optionExplanations.B: The index fingers do not demonstrate isolated Boutonnière deformity on both sides.
optionExplanations.C: Pronounced, severe ulnar deviation at the MCP joints is clearly evident across both hands.
optionExplanations.D: Per the source, the little finger of the left hand shows a boutonnière deformity: PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension from central slip attenuation and volar subluxation of the lateral bands. The patient photograph is not reproduced in the PDF.

questions.educationalObjective: Accurately recognize rheumatoid hand deformities: Boutonniere deformity consists of PIP joint flexion with compensatory DIP joint hyperextension secondary to central slip attenuation.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents with a painless, fluctuating swelling behind his right knee that has gradually increased in size over the past 4 months. He notes that the mass becomes noticeably tense and prominent after prolonged standing or walking, but becomes softer and smaller when resting supine with the knee flexed. On physical examination, a smooth, non-pulsatile, non-tender, cystic mass is palpable in the medial aspect of the popliteal fossa. Axial T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the knee reveals a hyperintense, thin-walled, fluid-filled cystic structure arising between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Deep vein thrombosis

questions.explanation:
A popliteal (Baker's) cyst is a benign, fluid-filled synovial distension of the bursa located between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle. In adults, Baker's cysts are virtually always secondary phenomena caused by underlying intra-articular knee pathology—most commonly medial meniscus tears or osteoarthritis. Increased intra-articular synovial fluid production coupled with knee motion forces fluid through a one-way 'check-valve' opening in the posteromedial capsule into the bursa. Characteristically, the cyst becomes firmer and more prominent during knee full extension (Foucher's sign) and softens during knee flexion. On MRI, it presents as a distinct, fluid-signal intensity sac with a characteristic 'neck' communicating directly between the semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius tendons.

High-yield clinical pearl: PSEUDOTHROMBOPHLEBITIS:
Acute rupture of a Baker's cyst spills synovial fluid into the calf muscle planes, mimicking acute deep vein thrombosis (calf erythema, tenderness, positive Homan sign, and distal crescent-shaped ankle hematoma). Duplex ultrasound is required to exclude DVT.

Exam trap: Never resect an adult Baker's cyst in isolation without treating the underlying intra-articular pathology (meniscal tear, chondral defect); otherwise, the cyst will inevitably recur.

optionExplanations.A: Popliteal artery aneurysm is a pulsatile vascular mass that demonstrates internal flow on duplex Doppler ultrasound rather than homogeneous cystic fluid.
optionExplanations.B: Lipomas are soft, solid mesenchymal adipose tumors that follow fat signal intensity (hyperintense on T1-weighted MRI) rather than fluid signal.
optionExplanations.C: A popliteal (Baker's) cyst is a herniated synovial fluid collection between the semimembranosus tendon and medial gastrocnemius, usually secondary to a meniscal tear or osteoarthritis, and it is firmer in extension and softer in flexion (Foucher's sign).
optionExplanations.D: Soft tissue sarcomas present as deep, enlarging, firm, solid masses that show heterogeneous contrast enhancement and invasive margins.
optionExplanations.E: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) causes diffuse unilateral calf edema, erythema, and pain without a discrete, well-circumscribed popliteal fossa mass; however, a ruptured Baker's cyst can mimic acute DVT (pseudothrombophlebitis).

questions.educationalObjective: Identify a popliteal (Baker's) cyst on physical exam and MRI by its classic posteromedial location between the semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius tendons, recognizing its etiology as a secondary manifestation of intra-articular knee pathology.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man sustained a displaced intra-articular tibial plateau fracture that was successfully treated with open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) achieving anatomic articular restoration and rigid stability. He healed uneventfully and enjoyed pain-free, active athletic function for 12 months. One year postoperatively, he presents with insidious, progressive joint pain exacerbated by weight-bearing, morning stiffness lasting 15 minutes, crepitus, and gradually declining range of motion. He has no fever, warmth, wound erythema, or systemic symptoms. Inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP) are entirely normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Malunion

questions.explanation:
This patient presents with classic features of post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) following an intra-articular fracture. Even when anatomic reduction and rigid fixation are achieved surgically, the initial mechanical trauma exerts catastrophic impact forces on the articular hyaline cartilage, causing acute chondrocyte necrosis, matrix microdamage, and subchondral microfractures. Over time, the compromised chondrocyte homeostasis, localized mechanical stress alterations, and release of catabolic inflammatory cytokines trigger progressive cartilage breakdown, leading to secondary osteoarthritis. Symptoms are characteristically mechanical: insidious joint pain exacerbated by activity/weight-bearing, brief morning stiffness (<30 minutes), crepitus, and gradual loss of range of motion in the absence of infectious or systemic inflammatory signs.

High-yield clinical pearl: PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF POST-TRAUMATIC OA:
High-energy intra-articular fractures cause immediate irreversible chondrocyte death (chondral shear/impact) and alters joint contact mechanics, precipitating premature secondary degenerative arthritis despite excellent surgical fixation.

Exam trap: Brief morning stiffness (<30 min) that worsens with activity is the hallmark of OSTEOARTHRITIS (degenerative), whereas prolonged morning stiffness (>45–60 min) that improves with activity indicates INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIS (e.g., RA).

optionExplanations.A: Septic arthritis presents acutely with severe joint effusion, erythema, intense resting pain, inability to bear any weight, high fever, and elevated ESR/CRP.
optionExplanations.B: Even after anatomic reduction and rigid fixation, the initial chondrocyte and matrix injury plus altered joint contact pressures lead to progressive post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.C: Avascular necrosis predominantly affects vulnerable vascular watershed regions (femoral head, scaphoid, talar dome), not typically the tibial plateau.
optionExplanations.D: Nonunion involves persistent fracture site motion, pain at the fracture site rather than the joint line, and radiographically visible unhealed fracture gap at 6–9 months.
optionExplanations.E: Malunion indicates healing in an unacceptable non-anatomical alignment, whereas the prompt explicitly states satisfactory anatomical reduction was achieved.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize post-traumatic osteoarthritis as a common long-term sequela of intra-articular fractures resulting from irreversible chondrocyte injury and altered joint contact pressures.

questions.section: Module 3: Soft Tissue & Upper Extremity Disorders
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with a 5-month history of intermittent numbness, burning, and paresthesias affecting the palmar aspect of her right thumb, index finger, middle finger, and radial half of the ring finger. She notes that her symptoms are characteristically worse at night, often waking her from sleep and requiring her to shake her hand out for relief. During physical examination, light percussive tapping performed over the volar aspect of the wrist directly proximal to the flexor retinaculum elicits an electric tingling sensation radiating into the index and middle fingers. Which of the following physical signs was demonstrated?
questions.explanation:
This clinical picture demonstrates Tinel's sign at the wrist, a provacative physical test used in the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). Tinel's sign is elicited by lightly tapping with the index finger or reflex hammer over the course of the median nerve at the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) on the volar aspect of the wrist. A positive response is the reproduction of tingling, paresthesias, or an electric shock-like sensation in the cutaneous distribution of the median nerve (volar surface of the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger). Carpal tunnel syndrome is the most common compressive neuropathy of the upper extremity, frequently associated with female sex, obesity, diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, and hypothyroidism.

High-yield clinical pearl: CARPAL TUNNEL SENSORY SPARING:
The PALMAR CUTANEOUS BRANCH OF THE MEDIAN NERVE branches approximately 5 cm proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum; therefore, SENSATION OVER THE THENAR EMINENCE IS SPARED IN CTS . Numbness involving the thenar eminence indicates compression proximal to the carpal tunnel (e.g., pronator teres syndrome or C6 radiculopathy).

Exam trap: Do not confuse Tinel's sign (percussion/tapping over nerve) with Phalen's maneuver (prolonged wrist flexion). Both test for CTS, but the mechanics differ.

optionExplanations.A: Allen's test evaluates the patency of the radial and ulnar arteries and the integrity of the superficial palmar arch prior to arterial puncture.
optionExplanations.B: Phalen's test reproduces median nerve paresthesias by holding the wrists in maximal passive unforced flexion (dorsa of hands pressed together) for 60 seconds.
optionExplanations.C: Tinel's sign, reproduction of tingling in the median nerve distribution when the nerve is tapped at the volar wrist, is the provocative test described for carpal tunnel syndrome.
optionExplanations.D: Finkelstein's test is pathognomonic for De Quervain's tenosynovitis (APL and EPB tendons), elicited by placing the thumb into the palm, making a fist, and sharply deviating the wrist ulnarly.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify Tinel's sign as light percussion over the median nerve at the volar wrist reproducing paresthesias in the median nerve distribution, indicating compressive neuropathy.

questions.section: Module 3: Soft Tissue & Upper Extremity Disorders
questions.question: A 42-year-old auto mechanic presents with a 2-month history of sharp, aching pain over the lateral aspect of his right dominant elbow that radiates distally into the dorsolateral forearm. The pain is noticeably aggravated whenever he forcefully grips screwdrivers or wrenches, and during manual wrist extension against resistance. On physical examination, there is maximal localized point tenderness approximately 1 cm distal and anterior to the lateral epicondyle, and pain is reproduced with resisted extension of the middle finger (Maudsley's test) and resisted wrist extension with the elbow in full extension (Cozen's test). Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.B: Rest, activity modification, and physical therapy exercises
options.C: Immediate surgery to repair the tendon
options.D: Doing nothing and continuing the painful activity
options.E: Putting the arm in a cast for two months

questions.explanation:
This patient presents with textbook lateral epicondylitis ('tennis elbow'), an overuse tendinopathy primarily involving angiofibroblastic tendinosis and microscopic tearing at the origin of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) muscle at the lateral humeral epicondyle. The clinical diagnosis is established by: 1. Discrete point tenderness over the ECRB origin on the lateral epicondyle. 2. Reproduction of pain with resisted wrist extension (Cozen's test) and resisted middle finger extension (Maudsley's test). 3. Pain exacerbated by repetitive wrist gripping, pronation, and extension. First-line management is strictly non-operative conservative therapy: temporary rest, activity modification, counterforce bracing (forearm strap), cryotherapy, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and structured physical therapy incorporating eccentric strengthening exercises of the forearm extensors. Over 90% of patients resolve successfully within 6 to 12 months.

High-yield clinical pearl: KEY ANATOMICAL MUSCLE INVOLVED:
EXTENSOR CARPI RADIALIS BREVIS (ECRB) is the primary muscle involved in lateral epicondylitis. In contrast, MEDIAL EPICONDYLITIS ('GOLFER'S ELBOW') involves the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis (FCR) origins.

Exam trap: Steroid injections may produce dramatic short-term relief at 4–6 weeks but have higher recurrence rates and worse 1-year clinical outcomes compared to physical therapy and watchful waiting.

optionExplanations.A: Frequent, long-term corticosteroid injections provide temporary short-term pain relief but carry significant long-term risks of tendon rupture, subcutaneous fat atrophy, skin depigmentation, and worse outcomes at 1 year.
optionExplanations.B: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) is an overuse tendinopathy of the ECRB origin, and initial management is conservative: rest, activity modification and physical therapy exercises.
optionExplanations.C: Surgical intervention (debridement of degenerated ECRB origin) is reserved only for refractory symptoms failing at least 6 months of dedicated conservative therapy.
optionExplanations.D: Continuing repetitive forceful aggravating tasks causes progressive microtearing and chronic tendinosis.
optionExplanations.E: Prolonged cast immobilization leads to joint stiffness, muscle atrophy, and does not address the underlying tendon degenerative pathology.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that lateral epicondylitis is an overuse tendinopathy of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) treated primarily with activity modification, eccentric physical therapy, and counterforce bracing.

questions.section: Module 3: Soft Tissue & Upper Extremity Disorders
questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with longstanding type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with persistent discomfort and functional limitation of her right hand. She reports that her right middle finger frequently gets stuck in a flexed posture, especially in the morning upon awakening, requiring her to use her left hand to manually snap or pop it back into full extension, which causes a painful clicking sensation. On physical examination, a small, tender, nodular thickening is palpated over the palmar aspect of the third metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint. When she flexes and extends the finger, the nodule is felt catching beneath a ligamentous structure. What is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?

options.A: Thickening of the flexor tendon sheath
options.C: Ulnar nerve compression at the elbow
options.D: Inflammation of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist

questions.explanation:
This patient presents with classic trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis), a condition characterized by a size mismatch between the flexor tendons (flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus) and the retinacular first annular (A1) pulley at the metacarpal head. Repetitive friction and inflammation lead to hypertrophy, fibrocartilaginous metaplasia, and thickening of the flexor tendon sheath (A1 pulley), often accompanied by the formation of a discrete nodule within the flexor tendon (Notta's node). During finger flexion, the strong flexor muscles pull the nodule proximally through the constricted A1 pulley. However, during extension, the weaker extensor mechanism cannot generate sufficient force to pull the enlarged nodule back through the stenotic sheath, causing the digit to lock in flexion. Trigger finger is significantly more prevalent in patients with diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, and amyloidosis. First-line medical therapy includes corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath; refractory cases undergo percutaneous or open A1 pulley release.

High-yield clinical pearl: PULLEY ANATOMY:
There are 5 annular pulleys (A1 to A5) and 3 cruciate pulleys (C1 to C3). The A1 PULLEY is the site of trigger finger pathology and can be safely divided surgically. In contrast, the A2 AND A4 PULLEYS are critical biomechanical pulleys that must NEVER be divided, as cutting them causes bowstringing of the flexor tendons.

Exam trap: Trigger finger involves the A1 PULLEY ON THE PALMAR ASPECT of the MCP joint. Do not confuse it with De Quervain's tenosynovitis, which involves the FIRST DORSAL COMPARTMENT at the radial styloid.

optionExplanations.A: Trigger finger results from thickening of the flexor tendon sheath (A1 pulley), often with a tendon nodule, which makes the tendon catch and lock in flexion.
optionExplanations.B: Extensor tendon rupture (such as mallet finger at the DIP or central slip rupture at the PIP) results in inability to extend the joint actively, but does not present with a palpable clicking palmar nodule catching beneath a pulley.
optionExplanations.C: Ulnar nerve compression at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome) causes numbness in the 4th and 5th digits and intrinsic hand muscle wasting, not digital triggering.
optionExplanations.D: Inflammation of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist is De Quervain's tenosynovitis, affecting the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) at the radial styloid, not the flexor tendons.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify trigger finger as a stenosing tenosynovitis caused by hypertrophy and thickening of the flexor tendon sheath at the A1 pulley, leading to mechanical entrapment of the flexor tendon.

questions.section: Module 4: Spine Pathology & Low Back Pain
questions.question: A 26-year-old software engineer and amateur weightlifter presents with acute, dull aching lower back pain that began 2 days ago after lifting heavy moving boxes. The pain is localized across the paraspinal muscles of the lumbar region without radiation into the buttocks or lower extremities. He denies bowel or bladder incontinence, saddle anesthesia, fever, unexplained weight loss, or history of malignancy. On physical examination, there is mild paraspinal muscular tenderness and spasm without midline spinal bony tenderness. Straight leg raise test is negative bilaterally, and deep tendon reflexes and motor strength are completely intact (5/5). Which of the following is the most common cause of back pain in young adults?
questions.explanation:
Mechanical low back pain secondary to muscular strain and ligamentous sprain accounts for more than 70% to 85% of all low back pain presentations in young adults. Acute paraspinal strain occurs following mechanical overexertion, improper lifting ergonomics, or repetitive twisting forces that exceed the load-bearing capacity of the erector spinae muscles, multifidus, and supporting lumbosacral ligaments. The condition is self-limiting, with over 90% of cases resolving spontaneously within 4 to 6 weeks. Management focuses on remaining active (avoiding prolonged bed rest), scheduled nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or acetaminophen, short-term muscle relaxants if severe spasm is present, and early physical therapy. Imaging (X-ray or MRI) is strictly NOT indicated in the absence of red flag symptoms.

High-yield clinical pearl: BED REST MYTH IN ACUTE LBP:
Prolonged strict bed rest (>48 hours) is detrimental; it leads to muscular deconditioning, joint stiffness, and delayed recovery. Early resumption of normal light physical activity within pain tolerance accelerates functional improvement.

Exam trap: Routine imaging (plain radiographs, CT, MRI) in uncomplicated acute mechanical low back pain (<6 weeks duration, no red flags) does NOT improve outcomes and exposes patients to unnecessary radiation and incidental findings.

optionExplanations.A: Muscle spasm and ligament sprain (mechanical strain) account for most low back pain in young adults and are self-limiting.
optionExplanations.B: Metastatic spine disease is exceptionally rare in young adults under 40 and typically occurs in older individuals (>50 years) with a known primary cancer (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid).
optionExplanations.C: Spinal fracture in young adults requires major high-energy axial trauma (fall from height, motor vehicle collision) or underlying metabolic bone disease.
optionExplanations.D: Spinal infections (vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, epidural abscess) are uncommon causes representing <1% of cases, typically seen in IV drug users, immunosuppressed patients, or following spinal instrumentation.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify lumbar muscle strain and ligamentous sprain as the overwhelmingly most common etiology of acute low back pain in young adults.

questions.section: Module 4: Spine Pathology & Low Back Pain
questions.question: A 45-year-old construction worker presents to the urgent care clinic with severe, progressive lower back pain. During the clinical evaluation, the physician systematically reviews the patient's history and physical examination findings to rule out sinister spinal pathology requiring urgent neurosurgical intervention or advanced imaging. Which of the following is considered a RED FLAG in the evaluation of low back pain?
questions.explanation:
The evaluation of low back pain relies on identifying 'red flag' clinical features that indicate serious underlying conditions such as spinal fractures, malignancy, spinal epidural abscess, or cauda equina syndrome. A history of recent significant trauma (e.g., motor vehicle crash, fall from height, or even minor low-energy falls in osteoporotic or elderly individuals) is a critical red flag warning of potential vertebral body compression fracture, burst fracture, or spinal column instability. Immediate plain radiography or computed tomography (CT) is indicated in the presence of recent trauma.

High-yield clinical pearl: CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME (SURGICAL EMERGENCY):
Combination of severe back pain, BILATERAL SCIATICA, SADDLE ANESTHESIA (S3–S5 dermatomes), URINARY RETENTION (overflow incontinence with post-void residual >200 mL), and lax anal sphincter tone. Requires emergency MRI and surgical decompression within 24–48 hours.

Exam trap: Mechanical back pain is aggravated by activity and relieved by rest. Malignant or infectious back pain is constant, persists at rest, and awakens the patient at night.

optionExplanations.A: Age less than 40 is a reassuring characteristic of benign mechanical back pain; red-flag age extremes are onset at age >50 (malignancy, fracture) or <18 (spondylolysis, infection).
optionExplanations.B: Pain that worsens with movement and spine loading is the classic hallmark of benign mechanical musculoskeltal strain.
optionExplanations.C: Pain relieved by recumbency and rest is typical of benign mechanical back pain; in contrast, pain that is unrelieved by rest or worsens at night (nocturnal pain) is a major red flag for spinal neoplasm or infection.
optionExplanations.D: A history of recent significant trauma is a red flag for vertebral fracture or spinal instability and calls for prompt imaging.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify a history of recent trauma as a primary red flag in low back pain requiring immediate radiographic evaluation to exclude spinal fracture.

questions.section: Module 5: Knee Sports Injury & Ligamentous Biomechanics
questions.question: A 17-year-old female gymnast sustains an acute lateral patellar dislocation during a twisting floor exercise. The patella is reduced in the field, and she is evaluated in the sports medicine clinic. In discussing the biomechanical stabilization of the patellofemoral joint and initial management strategies, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: The trochlear groove and MPFL are static stabilizers, quadriceps is a dynamic stabilizer, and most first-time acute dislocations are treated non-operatively
options.B: Patellar instability affects males 33% more often than females
options.C: The MPFL is the primary dynamic stabilizer, while quadriceps is the primary static stabilizer
options.D: First-time acute patellar dislocations usually require surgery regardless of recurrence or loose bodies

questions.explanation:
Patellofemoral stability is maintained by a complex interaction of bony architecture, passive ligamentous restraints, and active dynamic muscular forces: 1. Static stabilizers: The trochlear groove (bony architecture of the distal femur) and the medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL). The MPFL is the primary static restraint to lateral patellar displacement, providing 50% to 60% of total restraining force between 0° and 30° of knee flexion. 2. Dynamic stabilizers: The quadriceps muscle complex, particularly the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO), which dynamically pulls the patella medially during active contraction. 3. Treatment: Most first-time acute patellar dislocations without osteochondral fracture or loose bodies are managed non-operatively with brief immobilization in extension, protected weight-bearing, followed by progressive physical therapy focusing on VMO and core strengthening. Surgery (MPFL reconstruction) is indicated for recurrent instability or associated intra-articular osteochondral loose bodies.

High-yield clinical pearl: MPFL INJURY LOCATION:
In acute lateral patellar dislocation, the MPFL ruptures in over 90% of cases, most commonly at its femoral attachment site near the adductor tubercle (Bassett's sign: discrete tenderness over the medial epicondyle).

Exam trap: Never rush to surgery for a first-time acute patellar dislocation if radiographs show no osteochondral fractures. Conservative management is successful in 50–70% of first-time dislocators.

optionExplanations.A: The trochlear groove and the medial patellofemoral ligament are the static stabilizers, the quadriceps (especially the vastus medialis obliquus) is the dynamic stabilizer, and uncomplicated first-time dislocations are managed non-operatively.
optionExplanations.B: Patellar instability is substantially more common in females than males due to increased ligamentous laxity, higher Q-angle, and trochlear dysplasia.
optionExplanations.C: The MPFL is a static ligamentous stabilizer, whereas the quadriceps (VMO) is a dynamic muscular stabilizer.
optionExplanations.D: Routine immediate operative repair is NOT indicated for first-time dislocations unless an osteochondral loose body (>5 mm) requires fixation/removal.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand patellofemoral biomechanics: the trochlear groove and MPFL provide static stability, the quadriceps (VMO) provides dynamic stability, and uncomplicated first-time dislocations are treated non-operatively.

questions.section: Module 5: Knee Sports Injury & Ligamentous Biomechanics
questions.question: A 13-year-old adolescent boy who plays competitive soccer on a daily basis presents with a 3-month history of localized anterior knee pain and a prominent bump over his upper shin. The pain characteristically worsens during and immediately after sprinting, kicking, and jumping, but is reliably relieved by rest. On physical examination, there is pronounced point tenderness and localized soft-tissue swelling directly over the tibial tuberosity. The knee joint itself is stable with no effusion, joint line tenderness, or ligamentous laxity. Resisted active knee extension reproduces pain over the tibial tubercle. Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding this condition?

options.A: The patient must stop all physical activity permanently
options.B: This condition is self-limiting and improves after growth plate closure
options.D: Surgical excision of the tubercle is needed

questions.explanation:
This patient presents with classic Osgood-Schlatter disease (traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle). During the adolescent growth spurt (ages 10–15 years in boys), rapid longitudinal bone growth outpaces tendon elongation. Repetitive, forceful contraction of the quadriceps muscle during running, jumping, and kicking sports generates excessive tensile traction forces across the patellar tendon insertion onto the still-cartilaginous tibial secondary ossification center (apophysis). This leads to recurrent microavulsions, localized osteochondritis, and reparative heterotopic bone formation (causing the characteristic prominent, tender bump). The condition is fundamentally benign and self-limiting, resolving completely once the tibial physis and apophysis fuse at skeletal maturity (typically around ages 14–18). Management consists of conservative measures: activity modification within pain tolerance (no need for complete bed rest or permanent cessation), ice packs, hamstring stretching, and brief NSAIDs. Surgery is almost never indicated in adolescents.

High-yield clinical pearl: SINDING-LARSEN-JOHANSSON DISEASE:
The distal pole counterpart to Osgood-Schlatter! It is a traction apophysitis at the INFERIOR POLE OF THE PATELLA (proximal patellar tendon origin) in running/jumping adolescents.

Exam trap: Never inject steroids into or near the patellar tendon in pediatric or adult athletes—steroids degrade tendon collagen fibrils, leading to spontaneous rupture.

optionExplanations.A: Permanent cessation of sports is completely unnecessary; patients are encouraged to continue sports with temporary activity modification based on pain.
optionExplanations.B: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a self-limiting traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle that improves once the growth plate closes.
optionExplanations.C: Corticosteroid injections are strictly contraindicated around the patellar tendon due to the high risk of catastrophic patellar tendon rupture and subcutaneous fat atrophy.
optionExplanations.D: Surgical excision of ossicles is only rarely considered in skeletally mature adults with persistent symptomatic ununited intratendinous ossicles.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize Osgood-Schlatter disease as a benign, self-limiting traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle that improves spontaneously upon physis fusion at skeletal maturity.

questions.section: Module 5: Knee Sports Injury & Ligamentous Biomechanics
questions.question: A 25-year-old athlete is evaluated following a sports-related knee injury. The physician suspects an isolated tear of the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL). Which historical presentation and symptom pattern is most characteristic of an isolated posterior cruciate ligament injury compared to an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear?

options.A: No popping, gradual slow swelling over days, and patients are usually able to bear weight
options.B: No swelling, recurrent locking, and delayed inability to extend the knee
options.D: Loud pop and immediate swelling within 1 to 2 hours

questions.explanation:
The clinical presentation of an isolated posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear differs dramatically from that of an ACL tear: 1. Mechanism: PCL injuries typically occur from a direct anterior blow to the proximal tibia with the knee flexed (e.g., dashboard injury in a motor vehicle collision) or falling forward onto a flexed knee with the foot in plantarflexion. 2. Symptoms: Patients with isolated PCL tears frequently report vague, insidious, mild-to-moderate posterior knee aching. Crucially, they rarely hear or feel an audible 'pop', exhibit gradual, slow mild swelling over 24 to 48 hours (rather than tense acute hemarthrosis), and are usually able to bear weight and ambulate immediately after the injury. In stark contrast, patients with acute ACL ruptures classically report a loud audible 'pop', immediate severe pain, sudden instability/giving way, inability to bear weight, and rapid tense hemarthrosis within 2 to 6 hours.

High-yield clinical pearl: CLINICAL PEARL (ACL VS PCL PRESENTATION):
• ACL:
High energy non-contact pivot -> Loud POP -> Rapid tense hemarthrosis (<2-6 hrs) -> Inability to walk.
• PCL:
Anterior tibial blow/fall -> NO pop -> Mild insidious swelling (>24-48 hrs) -> Able to walk/bear weight.

Exam trap: Because patients with isolated PCL tears can often walk off the field, the injury is frequently missed acutely and presents months later as vague anterior knee pain (patellofemoral overload) during hill descent or stair climbing.

optionExplanations.A: An isolated PCL tear typically causes no audible pop, slow mild swelling over days, and the patient can usually bear weight, unlike an ACL tear.
optionExplanations.B: Recurrent locking, catching, and delayed inability to fully extend the knee ('locked knee') are pathognomonic for an unstable bucket-handle meniscal tear.
optionExplanations.C: Immediate severe hemarthrosis within hours is the hallmark of an acute ACL rupture or patellar dislocation, not isolated PCL tears.
optionExplanations.D: An audible 'loud pop' accompanied by immediate swelling is the classic presentation of an ACL tear (70% of acute traumatic knee hemarthroses).

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate PCL tears from ACL injuries by recognizing that isolated PCL tears characteristically present without an audible pop, with minimal/gradual swelling, and with preserved ability to bear weight.

questions.section: Module 5: Knee Sports Injury & Ligamentous Biomechanics
questions.question: A 21-year-old collegiate soccer player sustains a non-contact deceleration and pivoting twisting injury to her left knee during a match. She felt a loud pop followed by rapid swelling. Clinical examination confirms anterior laxity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the knee is performed to assess the extent of ligamentous and chondral injury. Which of the following MRI findings is most characteristically associated with an acute complete anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture?

options.C: Posterolateral bone bruise with an intact PCL
options.E: Angulation of the PCL indicates complete ACL disruption

questions.explanation:
During a non-contact pivot-shift injury (valgus stress, internal tibial rotation, and knee flexion), the tibia subluxates anteriorly relative to the femur as the ACL ruptures. As the knee reduces, the lateral femoral condyle (sulcus terminalis) violently collides with the posterolateral tibial plateau. This distinctive bone impact generates a pathognomonic 'kissing contusion' bone bruise pattern on MRI: hyperintense T2/STIR signal in the mid-lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau. This finding is present in more than 80% of acute complete ACL tears. In an isolated ACL rupture, the PCL remains structurally intact, though it may appear buckled or show an altered angle due to anterior displacement of the tibia.

High-yield clinical pearl: SEGOND FRACTURE:
An avulsion fracture of the lateral tibial plateau at the insertion of the anterolateral ligament (ALL), seen on plain AP radiograph. It is virtually pathognomonic (90–100% specific) for an underlying COMPLETE ACL RUPTURE.

Exam trap: Bone contusion location determines injury mechanism: POSTEROLATERAL TIBIA + LATERAL FEMORAL CONDYLE = ACL TEAR. ANTEROLATERAL FEMORAL CONDYLE + MEDIAL PATELLA = PATELLAR DISLOCATION.

optionExplanations.A: Complete PCL rupture does not occur in isolated non-contact pivoting ACL tears; combined ACL/PCL tears represent multiligamentous knee dislocations.
optionExplanations.B: Medial femoral condyle bone contusions are seen in lateral patellar dislocations (patellar impact against the lateral condyle) or direct blunt blows, not typical ACL non-contact pivot-shift kinematics.
optionExplanations.C: In a non-contact ACL rupture the lateral femoral condyle strikes the posterolateral tibial plateau, producing the characteristic posterolateral 'kissing contusion' bone bruise with the PCL intact.
optionExplanations.D: Isolated LCL tears are rare, caused by varus stress without rotation, and are not a feature of typical ACL injuries.
optionExplanations.E: While PCL buckling or increased curvature occurs secondary to anterior tibial translation, the primary characteristic bone bruise pattern is in the posterolateral compartment.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the characteristic 'kissing' bone contusion pattern of the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau on MRI as highly indicative of an acute ACL rupture.

questions.section: Module 5: Knee Sports Injury & Ligamentous Biomechanics
questions.question: An orthopedic sports medicine fellow conducts an evidence-based clinical physical examination seminar on anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears. She reviews the sensitivity, specificity, and biomechanical principles of the anterior drawer test, Lachman test, and pivot shift test. Which of the following statements regarding anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) physical examination is TRUE?

options.A: The anterior drawer test is the most sensitive clinical test for ACL injury
options.B: The pivot shift test is the most sensitive clinical test for ACL injury
options.C: Lachman test is the most sensitive clinical test, while the pivot shift test is the most specific
options.D: The posterior drawer test could be helpful

questions.explanation:
The diagnostic accuracy of physical examination maneuvers for acute ACL tears is firmly established in orthopedic literature: 1. Lachman test: Performed with the knee at 20° to 30° of flexion while translating the tibia anteriorly. It has a sensitivity of 85% to 95%, making it the single most sensitive clinical test for ACL tear. At 20–30° of flexion, the secondary restraints (hamstrings, posterior capsule) are relaxed, and the geometry of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus does not block anterior excursion. 2. Pivot shift test: Evaluates dynamic rotatory subluxation (anterolateral rotatory instability) by applying an internal rotation torque and valgus stress while moving the knee from extension into flexion. It boasts a specificity of 98% to 99%, making it the most specific clinical test (a positive pivot shift confirms an ACL rupture). However, its sensitivity is low in awake patients due to voluntary hamstring muscle guarding. 3. Anterior drawer test: Performed at 90° of flexion. Sensitivity is lower (50–70%) acutely because hamstring spasm, protective joint effusion, and wedging of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus against the femoral condyle physically prevent anterior translation.

High-yield clinical pearl: WHY LACHMAN BEATS ANTERIOR DRAWER:
At 90° flexion (drawer test), the posterior horn of the medial meniscus wedges like a doorstop against the medial femoral condyle, masking ACL laxity. At 20–30° (Lachman), this doorstop effect is disengaged.

Exam trap: Always evaluate the end-point: a normal ACL produces a crisp, solid 'hard' end-point. An ACL tear produces a mushy, soft, or absent end-point with increased excursion (>3 mm difference compared to normal contralateral knee).

optionExplanations.A: The anterior drawer test is significantly less sensitive than the Lachman test, especially in the acute setting.
optionExplanations.B: The pivot shift test has high specificity (98%) but poor sensitivity (often <40% without anesthesia) due to patient pain and guarding.
optionExplanations.C: The Lachman test is the most sensitive clinical test for ACL tear (about 85-95%) and the pivot shift test is the most specific (about 98-99%).
optionExplanations.D: The posterior drawer test specifically diagnoses PCL injuries, not ACL injuries.

questions.educationalObjective: Remember the diagnostic performance of ACL examination tests: the Lachman test is the most sensitive, while the pivot shift test is the most specific.

questions.section: Module 5: Knee Sports Injury & Ligamentous Biomechanics
questions.question: A 30-year-old motor vehicle collision unrestrained passenger sustains a dashboard injury to the anterior aspect of his right flexed knee. On physical examination, the orthopedic resident performs special ligamentous testing to evaluate for posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) disruption. Which of the following statements regarding posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury diagnosis is TRUE?

options.A: Lachman test is the gold standard for diagnosing PCL injury
options.B: Posterior sag sign is the gold standard for diagnosing PCL injury
options.C: The posterior drawer test is the gold standard for diagnosing PCL injury, with approximately 90% sensitivity and 99% specificity
options.D: Pivot shift test is the most specific test for PCL injury

questions.explanation:
The posterior drawer test is the established clinical gold standard for the evaluation and diagnosis of posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) ruptures, exhibiting an exceptional sensitivity of ~90% and specificity of ~99%. To perform the test, the patient is supine with the hip flexed to 45° and the knee flexed to 90°. The examiner sits on the patient's foot to stabilize the limb, ensures the hamstring tendons are completely relaxed, and applies a direct posterior force to the proximal tibia. Posterior tibial translation is graded based on the step-off relationship between the medial tibial plateau and the medial femoral condyle (normally the tibia sits 1 cm anterior to the femoral condyle): • Grade I: 1–5 mm posterior translation (tibia remains anterior to condyle). • Grade II: 6–10 mm translation (tibia flush with femoral condyle). • Grade III: >10 mm translation (tibia translates posterior to condyle; indicates combined PCL and posterolateral corner injury).

High-yield clinical pearl: FALSE-POSITIVE ANTERIOR DRAWER (THE PCL TRAP):
In a knee with a torn PCL, the tibia chronically sags posteriorly. If the examiner fails to recognize this starting position, pulling the tibia anteriorly simply brings it back to neutral, falsely interpreted as a positive anterior drawer (pseudo-ACL tear)!

Exam trap: Always assess the 1 cm normal anterior step-off of the medial tibial plateau before performing anterior or posterior drawer tests to avoid misdiagnosing a PCL tear as an ACL tear.

optionExplanations.A: The Lachman test evaluates the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), not the PCL.
optionExplanations.B: The posterior sag sign (Godfrey's test) is a valuable visual test where the tibia sags posteriorly under gravity at 90° flexion, but the posterior drawer test is the definitive gold standard manual maneuver.
optionExplanations.C: The posterior drawer test is the clinical gold standard for diagnosing PCL injury, with about 90% sensitivity and 99% specificity.
optionExplanations.D: The pivot shift test evaluates anterolateral rotatory instability from ACL deficiency, not PCL tears (the dial test or reverse pivot shift evaluates posterolateral corner/PCL injuries).

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the posterior drawer test as the gold standard clinical examination for PCL injury, with approximately 90% sensitivity and 99% specificity.

questions.section: Module 5: Knee Sports Injury & Ligamentous Biomechanics
questions.question: A 22-year-old basketball player lands awkwardly from a rebound, planting his foot firmly on the hardwood floor while cutting and forcefully twisting his torso. He experiences an immediate sharp tearing sensation along the medial joint line. Over the next 24 hours, he develops a modest effusion, accompanied by mechanical clicking and pain when squatting. Regarding meniscal tears, which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: They usually occur due to hyperextension of the knee
options.B: They commonly occur after a direct blow to the patella
options.C: They typically result from a twisting injury while the knee is flexed
options.D: They most commonly occur with the knee fully extended

questions.explanation:
The classic injury mechanism for a traumatic meniscal tear is a twisting (rotational) force applied to a flexed, weight-bearing knee. When the knee is flexed, the femoral condyles roll posteriorly onto the flat tibial plateau, and axial compression traps the fibrocartilaginous meniscus between the two articulating surfaces. Subsequent sudden internal or external rotation of the femur creates catastrophic shear stresses that exceed the tensile strength of the collagen fibers within the meniscus, resulting in longitudinal, radial, or bucket-handle tears. The medial meniscus is torn approximately three times more frequently than the lateral meniscus in non-contact sports injuries due to its firm peripheral attachment to the deep medial collateral ligament (MCL) and joint capsule, which renders it significantly less mobile.

High-yield clinical pearl: VASCULAR ZONES OF THE MENISCUS:
• RED-RED ZONE:
Outer 10–30% (rich peripheral blood supply from genicular arteries); excellent healing potential; amenable to primary surgical repair.
• WHITE-WHITE ZONE:
Inner 70% (completely avascular; nourished solely by synovial fluid diffusion); zero healing potential; requires partial meniscectomy when torn.

Exam trap: Bucket-handle tears of the medial meniscus can flip into the intercondylar notch, causing a true mechanical 'locked knee' (inability to achieve full terminal extension). This requires urgent arthroscopic reduction.

optionExplanations.A: Hyperextension of the knee typically injures the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) or causes posterior capsule strain, not isolated meniscal tears.
optionExplanations.B: A direct blow to the patella causes patellar fracture, patellofemoral cartilage contusion, or prepatellar bursitis, not meniscal tears.
optionExplanations.C: Traumatic meniscal tears result from a twisting force applied to a flexed, weight-bearing knee, which traps the meniscus between femur and tibia.
optionExplanations.D: In full extension, the knee is in its close-packed position with minimal rotational shear, rendering meniscal trapping far less likely than during flexion.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand the classic biomechanical mechanism of meniscal injury: a twisting rotational force applied to a flexed, weight-bearing knee.

questions.question: An orthopedic biomechanics researcher presents data on the primary and secondary stabilizers of the human knee joint during dynamic athletic tasks. Which of the following functional roles represents the primary biomechanical restraint provided by the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)?

options.A: Primary restraint to posterior tibial translation
options.B: Primary restraint to anterior tibial translation
options.C: Limitation of valgus stress at the knee
options.D: Prevention of meniscal displacement during knee flexion

questions.explanation:
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) provides 85% to 87% of the total passive restraint against anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur, establishing it as the undisputed primary static restraint to anterior tibial translation. The ACL originates from the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and inserts into the anterior intercondylar fossa of the tibia. It consists of two functional bundles: 1. Anteromedial (AM) bundle: Tightens in knee flexion; provides primary resistance to anterior translation during functional activities. 2. Posterolateral (PL) bundle: Tightens in knee extension; provides rotational stability (resists internal rotation and pivot-shift loads). Secondary restraints to anterior tibial translation include the collateral ligaments, iliotibial band, and the posterior horns of the menisci.

High-yield clinical pearl: CRUCIATE LIGAMENT BIOMECHANICS SUMMARY:
• ACL:
Primary restraint to Anterior tibial translation & internal rotational stability.
• PCL:
Primary restraint to Posterior tibial translation (strongest ligament in the knee).
• MCL:
Primary restraint to Valgus stress.
• LCL:
Primary restraint to Varus stress.

Exam trap: Remember that while the ACL resists rotational torque, its PRIMARY restraint (>85% of total resistance) is strictly ANTERIOR TIBIAL TRANSLATION.

optionExplanations.A: The primary restraint to posterior tibial translation is the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), providing ~95% of total restraint.
optionExplanations.B: The ACL provides about 85-87% of the passive restraint to anterior tibial translation, making it the primary restraint.
optionExplanations.C: The primary restraint to valgus stress at the knee is the medial collateral ligament (MCL).
optionExplanations.D: Meniscal motion is guided by the coronary ligaments, meniscofemoral ligaments (Humphry and Wrisberg), and popliteus tendon, not primarily by the ACL.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) as the primary biomechanical restraint to anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur.

questions.section: Module 5: Knee Sports Injury & Ligamentous Biomechanics
questions.question: An orthopedic surgeon is evaluating two distinct patient cohorts with meniscal pathology: young active athletes with traumatic tears versus older individuals with degenerative tears. Which of the following statements is CORRECT regarding meniscal tears and their underlying mechanics?

options.A: Traumatic meniscal tear is associated with rotational and compressive forces with the knee partially flexed
options.B: Degenerative meniscal tears are commonly caused by acute rotational and compressive forces in a young athlete
options.C: Traumatic meniscal tears usually occur with the knee fully extended and without rotational stress
options.D: Meniscal injuries most commonly result from hyperextension of the knee without axial loading
options.E: Degenerative meniscal tears are primarily associated with direct blows to the anterior aspect of the knee

questions.explanation:
Meniscal pathology is broadly dichotomized into two distinct clinical and biomechanical categories: 1. Traumatic meniscal tears: Characteristically occur in young, active athletic populations. The pathomechanics require a combination of axial compression (weight-bearing) and rotational (torsional) shear forces acting upon a partially flexed knee. This traps the mobile meniscal tissue between the femoral condyle and tibial plateau, shearing the collagen architecture (commonly causing vertical longitudinal or bucket-handle tears). 2. Degenerative meniscal tears: Occur in middle-aged or elderly individuals (>45–50 years) as an intrinsic component of generalized joint senescence and osteoarthritis. The meniscal fibrocartilage undergoes age-related desiccation, collagen fiber fragmentation, and cellular loss. These tears typically occur with minimal or no overt trauma (e.g., simply rising from a chair or kneeling) and manifest as complex, horizontal cleavage tears.

High-yield clinical pearl: MENISCAL TEAR PATTERNS:
• TRAUMATIC:
Young athletes -> Vertical, longitudinal, bucket-handle tears -> Good tissue quality -> Repair if in red-red zone.
• DEGENERATIVE:
Older patients (>50yo) -> Horizontal cleavage, complex tears -> Poor tissue quality -> Treat with physical therapy/conservative management first!
