Exam trap: Never rush an older patient with a degenerative meniscal tear to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy without a trial of physical therapy. Multiple randomized clinical trials show arthroscopy is no better than physical therapy for degenerative meniscal tears in osteoarthritis.

optionExplanations.A: Traumatic meniscal tears arise from combined axial compression and rotational forces on a partially flexed knee, whereas degenerative tears occur in older patients with little or no trauma.
optionExplanations.B: Degenerative tears occur in older adults with pre-existing cartilage fraying and wear, not from acute high-energy sports trauma in young athletes.
optionExplanations.C: Traumatic tears require rotational torsional stress and partial flexion; full extension minimizes rotational entrapment.
optionExplanations.D: Hyperextension without axial loading places stress on the ACL and posterior capsule, not the menisci.
optionExplanations.E: Degenerative tears are non-traumatic wear-and-tear phenomena, not the result of direct anterior blows.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate traumatic meniscal tears (rotational and compressive loading during partial knee flexion in athletes) from degenerative meniscal tears (horizontal wear in older arthritic knees).

questions.question: A concerned mother brings her 4-year-old son to the pediatric orthopedic clinic because she noticed that both of his feet appear completely flat without an arch when he stands on the floor. The child is entirely asymptomatic, keeps up with his peers on the playground, and runs without difficulty or pain. On physical examination, when the child stands on tiptoes, or when the examiner passively dorsiflexes the great toe (Jack's test), a normal, well-formed medial longitudinal arch immediately appears. Subtalar joint mobility is supple and full in all planes. Flexible flatfoot in children is best described as:

options.E: Associated with pain

questions.explanation:
Flexible flatfoot (physiologic pes planus) is an extremely common, benign developmental variation found in up to 90% of toddlers and 15–20% of adults due to physiologic ligamentous laxity and fat pad presence under the medial sole. The defining physical examination feature of a flexible flatfoot is that while the medial longitudinal arch collapses and disappears during full static weight-bearing, the arch reliably reconstitutes and becomes clearly visible when standing on tiptoes or during passive great toe dorsiflexion. This phenomenon is driven by the Windlass mechanism: dorsiflexing the hallux tightens the plantar fascia over the metatarsal head, elevating the medial longitudinal arch. Flexible flatfoot is painless, does not impair athletic function, and requires no active treatment, special orthotic shoes, or surgical intervention. Reassurance is the primary management.

High-yield clinical pearl: JACK'S TOE-RAISE TEST (WINDLASS TEST):
Passive dorsiflexion of the hallux tightens the plantar aponeurosis. If the arch reconstitutes -> Flexible flatfoot. If the arch remains flat and stiff -> Rigid flatfoot (order oblique foot radiographs to evaluate for tarsal coalition).

Exam trap: Do not prescribe expensive corrective shoe inserts or custom arch supports for painless flexible flatfoot in children— studies prove they do not alter the natural history of arch development and cause unnecessary financial stress for families.

optionExplanations.A: Tarsal coalition causes a rigid flatfoot, characterized by a permanently flattened arch that does NOT reconstitute on tiptoe and has restricted subtalar motion.
optionExplanations.B: Flexible flatfoot is a physiologic, non-pathological developmental stage in young children.
optionExplanations.C: In flexible flatfoot the arch collapses on standing but reappears on tiptoe or with passive great toe dorsiflexion (windlass mechanism); it is painless and needs only reassurance.
optionExplanations.D: Surgery is never indicated for asymptomatic flexible flatfoot.
optionExplanations.E: Physiologic flexible flatfoot is entirely painless; pain warrants a search for tarsal coalition, accessory navicular, or juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate flexible flatfoot from rigid flatfoot by noting that the arch reappears when standing on tiptoe due to the Windlass mechanism, representing a benign physiologic state requiring reassurance.

questions.question: A newborn infant is examined in the nursery. Physical examination of the left foot reveals a rigid, non-reducible deformity characterized by a convex, rounded plantar surface resembling the rocker of a rocking chair, severe hindfoot equinus and valgus, and dorsolateral dislocation of the midfoot with dorsiflexed forefoot resting against the anterior shin. Maximum plantarflexion cannot bring the midfoot into alignment. Congenital vertical talus presents with which of the following classic foot contours?
questions.explanation:
Congenital vertical talus (CVT), also known as congenital convex pes valgus, is an uncommon congenital foot deformity that classically presents with a 'rocker-bottom' foot. The underlying pathomorphology is a rigid, irreducible dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the head of the talus, locking the talus in a fixed, vertical, plantarflexed orientation. Key clinical features include: 1. Convex plantar contour (rocker-bottom appearance) with the vertically oriented talar head acting as the prominent pivot point on the plantar medial sole. 2. Rigid hindfoot equinus and valgus due to contracture of the Achilles tendon. 3. Rigid midfoot/forefoot dorsiflexion and abduction resting against the anterior tibia. CVT is frequently associated with neuromuscular disorders and genetic syndromes, including arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, myelomeningocele, and Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome).

High-yield clinical pearl: RADIOGRAPHIC CONFIRMATION OF CVT:
On maximum plantarflexion lateral radiograph, the long axis of the talus remains vertically oriented and fails to align with the first metatarsal (demonstrating fixed, non-reducible talonavicular dislocation).

Exam trap: Do not confuse CONGENITAL VERTICAL TALUS (rigid rocker-bottom foot; associated with Trisomy 18/arthrogryposis) with CALCANEOVALGUS FOOT (supple, hyper-dorsiflexed foot resting on shin; resolves spontaneously with gentle stretching).

optionExplanations.A: While the arch is absent, simple flatfoot lacks the rigid convex rocker-bottom contour and vertically oriented talus on lateral plantarflexion radiographs.
optionExplanations.B: Congenital vertical talus produces a rigid rocker-bottom foot from irreducible dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talar head.
optionExplanations.C: Claw toes represent hyperextension at the MTP joint and flexion at PIP/DIP joints, commonly seen in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
optionExplanations.D: High arch (pes cavus) is the polar opposite of a rocker-bottom foot, typically seen in neurological disorders like Friedreich's ataxia or CMT.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify congenital vertical talus as a rigid congenital deformity presenting with a pathognomonic rocker-bottom foot contour secondary to irreversible dorsal dislocation of the navicular on a vertical talus.

questions.question: A full-term male neonate is born with a unilateral congenital foot deformity. The orthopedic consultant performs a systematic structural examination of the infant's foot and ankle to categorize the components of clubfoot (congenital talipes equinovarus). Clubfoot is characterized by all of the following components EXCEPT:

options.E: Adduction

questions.explanation:
Congenital clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) is characterized by four cardinal, distinct anatomical deformities that are universally remembered by the medical mnemonic C-A-V-E: 1. C - Cavus: High medial longitudinal arch due to plantarflexion of the first metatarsal relative to the hindfoot. 2. A - Adductus: Medial deviation of the forefoot and metatarsals relative to the midfoot. 3. V - Varus: Inward tilting/inversion of the hindfoot (calcaneus). 4. E - Equinus: Plantarflexion of the ankle joint caused by severe contracture of the gastrocnemius-soleus-Achilles complex. The hindfoot is in VARUS, never valgus! Valgus is the exact opposite of the clubfoot deformity and is the correct answer to this EXCEPT question.

High-yield clinical pearl: PONSETI CORRECTION ORDER (C-A-V-E):
Correction must follow this precise sequence:
1. Correct Cavus first (supinate forefoot to align with hindfoot).
2. Correct Adductus and Varus simultaneously by abducting the foot in supination with a counter-pressure fulcrum on the lateral head of the talus.
3. Correct Equinus LAST (dorsiflex ankle; ~85-90% require percutaneous Achilles tenotomy under local anesthesia).

Exam trap: Never pronate the clubfoot! Pronation exacerbates the cavus deformity by jamming the calcaneus under the talus.

optionExplanations.A: Cavus is the 'C' in CAVE; it is corrected first in the Ponseti casting protocol.
optionExplanations.B: Varus is the 'V' in CAVE; the calcaneus is inverted beneath the talus.
optionExplanations.C: Equinus is the 'E' in CAVE; it is corrected last, frequently requiring a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy.
optionExplanations.D: Clubfoot consists of Cavus, Adductus, Varus and Equinus (CAVE); the hindfoot is in varus, never valgus, so valgus is the exception.
optionExplanations.E: Adduction is the 'A' in CAVE; the forefoot points medially toward the midline.

questions.educationalObjective: Memorize the C-A-V-E mnemonic for clubfoot: Cavus, Adductus, Varus, and Equinus; recognize that hindfoot valgus is NOT part of clubfoot.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the orthopedic clinic by his parents because of a persistent, painless antalgic limp for the past 4 weeks, which has recently evolved into mild ache localized to the groin and anterior thigh that worsens after soccer practice. On physical examination, internal rotation and abduction of the affected right hip are significantly restricted. Plain pelvis and frog-leg lateral radiographs demonstrate flattening, subchondral collapse (crescent sign), sclerosis, and distinct fragmentation of the right femoral capital epiphysis with widening of the joint space. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This clinical picture is diagnostic for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral capital epiphysis). Perthes disease predominantly affects boys between 4 and 8 years of age (male-to-female ratio 4:1). Patients characteristically present with an insidious, painless or minimally painful antalgic limp that worsens at the end of the day or after athletic activities, with referred pain to the groin, anterior thigh, or knee. Physical examination classically demonstrates restricted hip internal rotation and abduction. The natural history of Perthes follows four distinct radiographic stages (Waldenström classification): 1. Initial/Avascular stage: Sclerosis and joint space widening. 2. Fragmentation stage: Epiphyseal resorption, lucency, subchondral fracture (crescent sign), and fragmentation (as seen in this question). 3. Reossification stage: New woven bone replaces necrotic bone. 4. Healed/Remodeling stage: Reconstituted head (spherical vs aspherical congruency).

High-yield clinical pearl: PEDIATRIC HIP PATHOLOGY BY AGE GROUP:
• 0 TO 1 YEAR:
Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH).
• 2 TO 4 YEARS:
Transient Synovitis (toxic synovitis) vs Septic Arthritis.
• 4 TO 8 YEARS:
Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease (AVN; fragmentation).
• 10 TO 16 YEARS:
Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE; obese boys).

Exam trap: Knee pain in a child or adolescent must ALWAYS prompt a thorough examination and plain radiographs of the HIP; hip pathology routinely presents as isolated referred knee pain via the obturator nerve.

optionExplanations.A: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) presents in neonates or toddlers with leg length discrepancy, asymmetric thigh creases, and abnormal Ortolani/Barlow maneuvers, not with acute epiphyseal fragmentation at age 6.
optionExplanations.B: Septic arthritis is an acute emergency presenting with high fever, excruciating hip pain, absolute refusal to bear weight (Kocher criteria), and elevated inflammatory markers.
optionExplanations.C: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) occurs in obese adolescents aged 11–14, showing posterior displacement of the epiphysis relative to the femoral neck, not fragmentation in a 6-year-old.
optionExplanations.D: A boy aged 4-8 years with a painless limp, restricted internal rotation and abduction, and femoral epiphyseal flattening, sclerosis, crescent sign and fragmentation has Legg-Calve-Perthes disease.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease in a young boy (4–8 years) presenting with an antalgic limp, loss of internal rotation/abduction, and radiographic fragmentation of the femoral head.

questions.question: A pediatric orthopedic surgeon delivers a lecture on adolescent hip emergencies. She highlights the biomechanical and endocrinologic predisposing factors that lead to shear displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis across the hypertrophic zone of the physis. Which of the following patient profiles represents the classic and most significant epidemiological risk factor for slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)?
questions.explanation:
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is the most common adolescent hip disorder, characterized by a Salter-Harris type I fracture/displacement of the femoral head posteriorly and inferiorly through the hypertrophic zone of the proximal femoral growth plate. The classic demographic profile and single greatest risk factor is an obese adolescent male (ages 11 to 14 years). Pathophysiologically, excessive biomechanical body weight acting on an obliquely oriented physis during the peak pubertal growth spurt exerts immense shear stress that overcomes physeal structural stability. Endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency/excess, panhypopituitarism) alter physeal matrix strength and represent major secondary causes (especially if SCFE presents before age 10 or bilaterally). Clinically, the patient presents with a limping gait, groin or referred knee/thigh pain, and the affected leg rests in an obligatory external rotation posture during passive hip flexion.

High-yield clinical pearl: OBLIGATORY EXTERNAL ROTATION SIGN:
When the clinician passively flexes the patient's hip, the thigh spontaneously and involuntarily rotates externally. This physical finding is virtually pathognomonic for SCFE.

Exam trap: SCFE is an orthopedic urgency! As soon as SCFE is suspected or diagnosed, the patient must be made STRICTLY NON-WEIGHT-BEARING (WHEELCHAIR/CRUTCHES) IMMEDIATELY to prevent catastrophic acute unstable slip or complete vascular compromise. Treatment is urgent in situ percutaneous single-screw fixation.

optionExplanations.A: SCFE has a pronounced male predominance (male-to-female ratio 1.5:1 to 2:1).
optionExplanations.B: Underweight habitus is protective against the shear stresses that precipitate SCFE; obesity (>90th percentile BMI) is present in >70% of affected patients.
optionExplanations.C: SCFE classically affects obese adolescent males aged about 11-14 years, when body weight acting on an obliquely oriented physis during the growth spurt produces shear.
optionExplanations.D: SCFE typically occurs during the rapid pubertal growth spurt, not during periods of slow growth.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify an obese adolescent male undergoing a pubertal growth spurt as the prototypical high-risk patient for slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).

questions.question: A 3-month-old female infant is brought for a well-child checkup. The pediatrician detects asymmetric gluteal thigh skin folds and a subtle positive Barlow maneuver in the left hip. The physician orders diagnostic imaging to evaluate for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). Which of the following imaging modalities is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of DDH in an infant under 4 to 6 months of age?
questions.explanation:
Ultrasonography (Graf technique) is the undisputed imaging modality of choice for diagnosing developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in infants under 4 to 6 months of age. In early infancy (<4–6 months), the femoral head and the acetabulum are composed predominantly of unossified radiolucent cartilaginous tissue. Because cartilaginous structures cannot be visualized on plain radiographs (X-rays), plain radiographs have poor diagnostic utility and high false-negative rates in young infants prior to the appearance of the femoral head secondary ossification center (which typically ossifies between 4 and 7 months). Ultrasound provides dynamic, high-resolution, radiation-free anatomical imaging that directly visualizes the cartilaginous femoral head, acetabular labrum, and coverage (alpha and beta angles). After 6 months of age, plain anteroposterior pelvis radiographs become the primary diagnostic investigation.

High-yield clinical pearl: DDH IMAGING TIMELINE:
• AGE < 4 TO 6 MONTHS:
DYNAMIC ULTRASOUND (investigation of choice).
• AGE > 4 TO 6 MONTHS:
AP PELVIS RADIOGRAPH (evaluates Hilgenreiner's line, Perkin's line, and Shenton's line once the ossification center appears).

Exam trap: Do not perform screening hip ultrasound prior to 4 TO 6 WEEKS OF LIFE in newborns with mild laxity, because physiologic maternal ligamentous laxity produces high rates of false-positive transient instability that spontaneously resolves.

optionExplanations.A: Plain radiographs are unreliable prior to 4–6 months because the unossified cartilaginous femoral head is invisible; radiographs become primary only after 6 months.
optionExplanations.B: In infants under 4-6 months the femoral head is unossified cartilage, so ultrasound (Graf technique) is the investigation of choice for DDH.
optionExplanations.C: Computed tomography (CT) exposes the infant to significant ionizing radiation and is reserved for evaluating reduction confirmation inside a spica cast after closed/open reduction.
optionExplanations.D: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) requires general anesthesia or sedation in infants; it is reserved for complex surgical planning, not initial screening or diagnosis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize ultrasonography as the primary diagnostic imaging modality for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in infants younger than 4 to 6 months.

questions.question: A neonatologist performs a routine newborn screening examination at 24 hours of life. With the infant supine, the examiner grasps the thighs with the fingers over the greater trochanters and the thumbs over the inner thighs. While gently abducting the hips, the examiner lifts the greater trochanters anteriorly and feels a distinct, palpable 'clunk' as the femoral head relocates back into the acetabulum. A positive Ortolani test is diagnostic of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
A positive Ortolani test is pathognomonic for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) with a dislocated, reducible femoral head. The Ortolani maneuver is a reduction maneuver: 1. The infant is placed supine with hips flexed to 90°. 2. The examiner gently abducts the hips while simultaneously lifting the greater trochanter anteriorly. 3. If the hip is dislocated, this maneuver lifts the dislocated femoral head over the posterior acetabular rim, popping it back into the acetabular cup with a palpable, sensation-rich 'clunk' of reduction. In contrast, the Barlow test is a provocative dislocating maneuver: starting with a reduced hip, the examiner adducts the hip and applies gentle posterior pressure to see if the hip subluxates or dislocates out of the acetabulum.

High-yield clinical pearl: MNEMONIC FOR HIP EXAM IN DDH:
• Barlow = Back (pushes hip back and OUT; dislocates).
• Ortolani = Open (abducts hips and pops hip IN; reduces).

Exam trap: High-pitched benign ligamentous 'clicks' are ubiquitous in normal neonates and have no clinical significance; a true positive Ortolani or Barlow is a distinct, low-pitched, palpable 'CLUNK' of femoral head translation.

optionExplanations.A: A palpable clunk as the dislocated femoral head relocates during hip abduction with anterior lift of the trochanters is a positive Ortolani test, diagnostic of DDH.
optionExplanations.B: Perthes disease presents in children aged 4–8 years, well past infancy, and does not exhibit an Ortolani clunk.
optionExplanations.C: SCFE occurs in adolescents (ages 11–14 years) and is characterized by restricted internal rotation, not Ortolani reducibility.
optionExplanations.D: Congenital vertical talus is a foot deformity producing a rocker-bottom contour and has no relation to hip reduction tests.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the Ortolani test as the classic clinical maneuver for reducing a dislocated femoral head back into the acetabulum in developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).

questions.question: A 2-week-old neonate with severe idiopathic congenital clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) is evaluated in the pediatric orthopedic clinic. The parents are anxious and inquire about the standard, evidence-based gold-standard management protocol to achieve a functional, plantigrade, pain-free foot. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for clubfoot?
questions.explanation:
The Ponseti method (serial corrective casting) is the universally accepted, gold-standard treatment of choice for congenital clubfoot worldwide, with initial success rates exceeding 90% to 95%. Developed by Dr. Ignacio Ponseti, this method relies on the biological plasticity of infant connective tissue: 1. Serial long-leg casting: Initiated in the first weeks of life. Gentle weekly manual manipulations and plaster cast applications systematically correct the components in order: first cavus, then forefoot adduction and hindfoot varus simultaneously, using the lateral head of the talus as a fixed fulcrum. 2. Percutaneous Achilles Tenotomy: Required in ~85–90% of cases to completely correct residual hindfoot equinus, performed under local anesthesia in the clinic. 3. Bracing (Mitchell-Ponseti abduction bar): Worn 23 hours/day for 3 months, then during naps and night-time until age 4 to 5 years to prevent disease relapse. Extensive open surgical releases (posteromedial release) have been virtually abandoned due to high rates of long-term foot stiffness, arthrofibrosis, and weakness.

High-yield clinical pearl: KEY TO PREVENTING RELAPSE IN CLUBFOOT:
COMPLIANCE WITH THE FOOT ABDUCTION BRACE (BOOTS AND BAR) . Relapse rates approach 80% if bracing is discontinued prematurely; adherence until age 4–5 ensures permanent remodeling of the tarsal bones.

Exam trap: Never attempt to correct equinus by forceful dorsiflexion before hindfoot varus is fully corrected; doing so causes a 'rocker-bottom' iatrogenic deformity (breaking the foot through the midtarsal joint).

optionExplanations.A: Ponseti serial manipulation and casting, with percutaneous Achilles tenotomy when needed and abduction bracing, is the gold-standard treatment for clubfoot.
optionExplanations.B: Extensive surgical release at birth is strictly obsolete; surgical clubfoot interventions lead to severe long-term scarring, rigid painful feet, and early degenerative osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.C: 'Conservative' is non-specific; the precise, structured protocol is the Ponseti technique of serial manipulation, casting, tenotomy, and bracing.
optionExplanations.D: Orthosis alone cannot overcome the dense contractures of clubfoot; bracing is strictly used to maintain correction *after* casting, not to achieve initial reduction.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the Ponseti technique (serial weekly manipulative casting followed by percutaneous Achilles tenotomy and maintenance abduction bracing) as the gold-standard treatment of choice for congenital clubfoot.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy presents with progressive bilateral foot and ankle pain that worsens during soccer games. His parents note that he has had flat feet for several years, but recently his ankles feel stiff, and he frequently trips. On physical examination, both feet display marked flattening of the medial longitudinal arch that does NOT reconstitute when standing on tiptoes or during passive great toe extension. Subtalar joint inversion and eversion are severely restricted and rigid bilaterally, and active eversion elicits peroneal muscle spasm. Plain radiographs reveal an osseous bar bridging the calcaneus and navicular. Which of the following conditions is characteristically associated with rigid pes planus?
questions.explanation:
Tarsal coalition is the classic, prototypical cause of a rigid (stiff) flatfoot (also termed peroneal spastic flatfoot) in adolescents. Tarsal coalition represents an abnormal congenital failure of segmentation resulting in an abnormal bridge—either fibrous (syndesmosis), cartilaginous (synchondrosis), or bony (synostosis)—between two or more tarsal bones. The two most common varieties are: 1. Calcaneonavicular coalition (typically becomes symptomatic around ages 8–12 when the cartilaginous bridge ossifies). 2. Talocalcaneal coalition (involving the middle facet/sustentaculum tali; becomes symptomatic around ages 12–16). Symptoms develop during puberty as ossification eliminates subtalar motion, transferring abnormal compensatory stresses to the midtarsal joints. Examination confirms a rigid flatfoot with profound absence of subtalar inversion/eversion and reactive peroneal muscle spasm. CT scanning is the gold standard for defining coalition anatomy.

High-yield clinical pearl: KEY RADIOGRAPHIC SIGNS OF TARSAL COALITION:
• ANTEATER NOSE SIGN:
Elongation of the anterior superior calcaneal process on 45° internal oblique radiograph (Calcaneonavicular).
• C-SIGN:
Continuous C-shaped halo line formed by the medial talar dome and sustentaculum tali on lateral view (Talocalcaneal).

Exam trap: Whenever an adolescent presents with recurrent 'ankle sprains' or foot pain with a stiff, non-yielding subtalar joint, suspect tarsal coalition and order a 45° internal oblique foot radiograph or CT.

optionExplanations.A: Pes cavus is an abnormally high arch, the exact anatomical opposite of flatfoot.
optionExplanations.B: Congenital vertical talus causes a rigid rocker-bottom foot at birth, whereas tarsal coalition presents insidiously in older children and adolescents (8–14 years).
optionExplanations.C: Limping is a non-specific clinical symptom, not an underlying pathological condition or disease entity.
optionExplanations.D: Tarsal coalition (here a calcaneonavicular bar) causes a rigid, peroneal spastic flatfoot with absent subtalar motion that does not correct on tiptoe.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify tarsal coalition as the primary etiology of rigid, painful flatfoot with restricted subtalar joint motion and peroneal muscle spasm in adolescents.

questions.question: An orthopedic infectious disease team evaluates a bone biopsy and tissue aspirate from a focus of acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in a pediatric long bone. The diagram in the source document demonstrates the routes of spread of osteomyelitis: epiphyseal, intra-articular, subperiosteal, soft tissues, and intraosseous. In assessing the localized microenvironmental milieu within an established intraosseous sequestrum and abscess cavity, which of the following is the correct physiological characteristic of osteomyelitis?

options.A: Localized abscess with decreased pH and decreased PO2
options.B: Diffuse cellulitis with increased pH and increased PO2
options.C: Diffuse abscess with decreased pH and increased PO2
options.D: Localized abscess with increased pH and decreased PO2
options.E: Localized abscess with normal pH and normal PO2

questions.explanation:
Osteomyelitis begins in the highly vascular, hairpin-loop venous sinusoidal network of the metaphysis in growing children (where sluggish blood flow facilitates bacterial seeding, predominantly Staphylococcus aureus). As bacteria proliferate, polymorphonuclear leukocytes (neutrophils) migrate into the rigid unyielding intraosseous space. The ensuing inflammatory cascade produces progressive intraosseous pressure, thrombosis of nutrient vessels, and liquefactive bone necrosis, creating a localized intraosseous abscess. The metabolic microenvironment within an established osteomyelitic abscess is defined by two cardinal features: 1. Markedly Decreased pH (Severe Acidosis): Accelerated anaerobic glycolysis by dying neutrophils, necrotic debris, and bacteria leads to massive lactic acid accumulation (often dropping local pH to <5.5–6.0). 2. Markedly Decreased PO2 (Severe Hypoxia): Microvascular occlusion and thrombosis starve the focus of oxygen. This acidic, hypoxic, hypoperfused sanctuary dramatically impairs host neutrophil oxidative killing and renders many standard antibiotics (particularly aminoglycosides) ineffective.

High-yield clinical pearl: KEY ANATOMICAL STRUCTURES IN CHRONIC OSTEOMYELITIS:
• SEQUESTRUM:
Devitalized, avascular necrotic bone segment separated from living bone.
• INVOLUCRUM:
Sleeve of new reactive periosteal bone formed around the sequestrum.
• CLOACA:
An opening in the involucrum through which pus/sequestrum drains into soft tissue sinus tracts.

Exam trap: Antibiotic penetration: Aminoglycosides require an alkaline, aerobic environment for active transport into bacterial cells. In acidic, hypoxic osteomyelitic abscesses, aminoglycosides lose their bactericidal potency!

optionExplanations.A: An established osteomyelitic abscess is a localized collection with decreased pH (lactic acidosis) and decreased PO2 (hypoxia from vascular thrombosis).
optionExplanations.B: Osteomyelitis is an intraosseous infectious process, not a diffuse superficial cellulitis, and tissue PO2/pH are profoundly reduced, not increased.
optionExplanations.C: Abscesses are localized enclosed pockets of purulence and PO2 is profoundly depressed due to ischemia.
optionExplanations.D: Local tissue pH is intensely acidic (decreased), never increased (alkalotic).
optionExplanations.E: Normal physiological parameters cannot exist within an enclosed suppurative bacterial infection.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand the pathophysiology of osteomyelitis: suppuration within rigid bone causes vascular occlusion, forming a localized abscess characterized by profound acidosis (decreased pH) and tissue hypoxia (decreased PO2).

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 48 hours after sustaining an accidental deep needle-stick puncture wound to the volar aspect of her right index finger while sewing. Over the past 24 hours, she has experienced throbbing pain, swelling, and fever. On examination, the index finger exhibits uniform, symmetric 'sausage-digit' swelling throughout its entire length, is held in a slightly flexed posture at rest, demonstrates exquisite tenderness along the entire anatomical course of the flexor tendon sheath, and elicits agonizing, excruciating pain upon passive extension of the digit. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent surgical irrigation and debridement of the flexor tendon sheath combined with intravenous antibiotics
options.B: Aspiration of the swollen finger followed by oral antibiotics
options.E: Oral antibiotics and follow-up after one week

questions.explanation:
This patient exhibits all four of Kanavel's four cardinal signs of acute infectious flexor tenosynovitis (purulent tenosynovitis): 1. Symmetrical, uniform fusiform swelling of the entire digit ('sausage digit'). 2. Flexed posture of the finger at rest (minimizes intra-sheath pressure and pain). 3. Tenderness along the entire anatomical course of the flexor tendon sheath (from the distal phalanx to the distal palmar crease). 4. Severe, agonizing pain elicited by passive extension of the digit (the earliest and most sensitive sign). Infectious flexor tenosynovitis is a closed-space orthopedic surgical emergency! The closed fibro-osseous canal creates high compartment-like pressures that rapidly thrombose the delicate vincula tendinum (nutrient blood supply to the flexor tendons), leading to irreversible tendon ischemia, tendon rupture, and spreading deep fascial space infection (midpalmar/thenar spaces, space of Parona). Immediate treatment requires urgent open or catheter-directed surgical irrigation and debridement in the operating room combined with intravenous broad-spectrum bactericidal antibiotics (targeting Staph aureus and Streptococci).

High-yield clinical pearl: MOST SENSITIVE KANAVEL SIGN:
PAIN WITH PASSIVE EXTENSION is the single most sensitive early physical finding. The patient will scream in pain even with slight extension of the DIP/PIP joint.

Exam trap: Never treat Kanavel flexor tenosynovitis with oral antibiotics! It requires admission, immediate IV antibiotics, and urgent surgical operative drainage.

optionExplanations.A: Kanavel's signs indicate acute pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, a closed-space surgical emergency that needs urgent sheath irrigation and debridement plus intravenous antibiotics.
optionExplanations.B: Needle aspiration of the flexor sheath in the clinic is inadequate, risks tendon laceration, and cannot decompress the purulent fibro-osseous tunnel.
optionExplanations.C: NSAIDS and observation will lead to rapid digital necrosis, flexor tendon sloughing, and inevitable amputation.
optionExplanations.D: Reassurance is medical malpractice in the presence of a limb-threatening closed-space infection.
optionExplanations.E: Oral outpatient antibiotics are completely ineffective for suppurative tenosynovitis and guarantee permanent tendon necrosis.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify acute infectious flexor tenosynovitis by Kanavel's four cardinal signs and recognize the mandatory requirement for urgent surgical irrigation/debridement and IV antibiotics.

questions.question: An orthopedic team reviews why acute bacterial septic arthritis is classified as a true surgical emergency that mandates emergent decompression within hours. Why does delayed or inadequate treatment of septic arthritis result in permanent joint disability and rapid joint destruction?

options.A: Progressive chondrolysis and increased intra-articular pressure causes synovial perfusion compromise
options.B: Cartilage is regenerable but bone underneath is in risk of avascular necrosis
options.C: Septic arthritis is not an orthopedic emergency from the start. It is an overrated medical problem
options.D: Most cases of septic arthritis cases progress to chronic osteomyelitis which is the principal cause of disability
options.E: The main factor is the muscle necrosis, when the pus extends outside the capsule

questions.explanation:
Septic arthritis causes rapid, catastrophic, and irreversible joint destruction within 24 to 48 hours through a dual pathophysiological mechanism: 1. Enzymatic Chondrolysis: Bacteria (predominantly Staphylococcus aureus) and invading host neutrophils release potent proteolytic enzymes, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), elastases, and bacterial toxins that rapidly digest the extracellular proteoglycan and type II collagen framework of articular hyaline cartilage. 2. Increased Intra-Articular Pressure & Tamponade: The massive, rapid accumulation of purulent synovial effusion within an unyielding fibrous joint capsule produces extreme intra-articular pressures. When intracapsular pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, it creates an articular tamponade effect, compressing the subsynovial capillary microvasculature and lateral epiphyseal retinacular vessels (particularly in the hip). This compromises synovial nutrition and blood supply, starving the avascular hyaline cartilage and precipitating ischemic chondrocyte death and avascular necrosis (AVN) of the epiphysis. Because adult hyaline articular cartilage has zero regenerative capacity, the resulting joint destruction is permanent.

High-yield clinical pearl: KOCHER CRITERIA FOR PEDIATRIC SEPTIC ARTHRITIS OF THE HIP:
1. Inability to bear weight.
2. Temperature > 38.5°C (101.3°F).
3. ESR > 40 mm/hr.
4. WBC > 12,000/μL. (4/4 criteria present = >99% probability of septic arthritis; warrants emergent arthrotomy/arthroscopy).

Exam trap: Never delay surgical drainage while waiting for blood or synovial culture results if the joint aspirate is purulent (WBC >50,000/μL with >75–90% neutrophils). Permanent chondrolysis occurs in under 24–48 hours!

optionExplanations.A: Enzymatic chondrolysis plus raised intra-articular pressure that compromises synovial perfusion rapidly and irreversibly destroys the joint.
optionExplanations.B: Articular hyaline cartilage is completely avascular and cannot regenerate; once destroyed, it is replaced only by inferior fibrocartilage.
optionExplanations.C: Septic arthritis is universally acknowledged as a surgical orthopedic emergency; untreated, it causes permanent joint destruction, septic shock, and mortality.
optionExplanations.D: While osteomyelitis can rarely occur by contiguous spread, the primary cause of permanent joint destruction is direct enzymatic chondrolysis and tamponade-induced cartilage necrosis within hours, not delayed chronic osteomyelitis.
optionExplanations.E: Muscle necrosis is not the primary driver of intra-articular joint destruction.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain why septic arthritis destroys joints rapidly: bacterial/neutrophil enzymatic chondrolysis combined with high intra-articular pressure compromising synovial microvascular perfusion.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman with a history of right total knee arthroplasty performed 2 years ago presents with persistent, worsening pain, stiffness, and sinus tract drainage. Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated serum ESR and CRP. Synovial fluid aspiration confirms a periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) with biofilm-forming methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). The orthopedic surgical team plans a two-stage exchange arthroplasty. Which statement regarding the management of infection associated with joint arthroplasty is CORRECT?

options.A: Positive cultures after treatment usually allow immediate reimplantation
options.B: Laboratory abnormalities are highly specific, so aspiration is unnecessary once CRP is elevated
options.C: Gram-negative infections usually permit earlier reimplantation than gram-positive infections
options.D: Cement spacer impregnated with antibiotics is usually implanted at the initial debridement

questions.explanation:
The gold-standard surgical protocol for chronic periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) in North America is a two-stage exchange arthroplasty: 1. Stage 1: Complete explantation and removal of all foreign prosthetic hardware and polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement, radical debridement of infected synovium and devitalized bone, followed by implantation of an articulating or static PMMA cement spacer impregnated with high-dose heat-stable bactericidal antibiotics (typically Vancomycin and Tobramycin/Gentamicin). The antibiotic-loaded spacer serves two vital roles: it elutes extremely high local concentrations of antibiotics directly into the dead space without systemic toxicity, and it maintains soft tissue tension, leg length, and joint alignment. 2. Interval: 6 weeks of tailored systemic pathogen-specific intravenous antibiotics. 3. Stage 2: Once clinical signs, serologic markers (ESR, CRP), and repeat joint aspiration confirm eradication of infection, the patient undergoes spacer removal and revision reimplantation of the new permanent prosthesis.

High-yield clinical pearl: BACTERIAL BIOFILM IN PJI:
Bacteria form a thick extracellular polysaccharide slime matrix (biofilm) on metallic and polyethylene implants. Within the biofilm, sessile bacteria enter a metabolically dormant phase that is up to 1,000 times more resistant to systemic antibiotics, mandating complete hardware removal in chronic infections (>3-4 weeks).

Exam trap: Do not attempt Debridement, Antibiotics, and Implant Retention (DAIR) in chronic PJI (>3 weeks from index surgery or >3 weeks of symptoms); mature biofilm makes DAIR failure rates exceed 70–80%. Complete removal and antibiotic spacer placement is required.

optionExplanations.A: Persistently positive cultures or elevated inflammatory markers represent active ongoing infection, which absolutely contraindicates reimplantation.
optionExplanations.B: Serum ESR and CRP are sensitive screening tests, but they are not specific; sterile joint aspiration for synovial fluid WBC count, differential (% PMNs), leukocyte esterase, and cultures is mandatory to confirm PJI.
optionExplanations.C: Gram-negative (e.g., Pseudomonas) and fungal infections form resistant biofilms and are difficult to eradicate, often requiring prolonged courses and having lower reimplantation success rates.
optionExplanations.D: In a two-stage exchange for periprosthetic infection, the first stage removes the prosthesis and cement and implants an antibiotic-impregnated cement spacer.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the key component of two-stage exchange arthroplasty for chronic periprosthetic joint infection: radical debridement, prosthesis explantation, and placement of an antibiotic-impregnated cement spacer.

questions.question: A 6-year-old previously healthy boy is admitted to the pediatric orthopedic service with a 4-day history of high fever (39.2°C), localized severe pain, refusal to bear weight, and soft-tissue warmth over the proximal tibial metaphysis. Blood cultures grow methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), and MRI confirms acute hematogenous osteomyelitis without subperiosteal abscess. What is the most appropriate antibiotic duration and regimen?

options.C: 3 weeks IV antibiotics followed by 3 weeks oral antibiotics

questions.explanation:
The traditional and evidence-based therapeutic regimen for uncomplicated pediatric acute hematogenous osteomyelitis has historically been a total of 4 to 6 weeks of bactericidal antimicrobial therapy. In classic university examination curricula, the standard established protocol consists of an initial intensive intravenous phase followed by an oral consolidation phase, classically taught as 3 weeks of intravenous antibiotics followed by 3 weeks of high-dose oral antibiotics (total 6 weeks of therapy), transitioning to oral once the child is afebrile, clinically improved, and CRP is down-trending. (Note: While modern pediatric infectious disease guidelines permit earlier transition to high-dose oral therapy at 3–7 days if clinical improvement and CRP reduction are documented, Option C represents the authoritative classic curriculum answer key ensuring complete eradication and preventing chronic recrudescent osteomyelitis).

High-yield clinical pearl: PRIMARY CAUSATIVE ORGANISM:
STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS is the single most common causative organism across all age groups. In infants <2 months, add coverage for Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae) and Gram-negative bacilli. In patients with sickle cell disease, cover SALMONELLA and S. aureus.

Exam trap: Serum C-REACTIVE PROTEIN (CRP) is the most sensitive and reliable laboratory marker for monitoring treatment response in acute osteomyelitis (normalizes within 1–2 weeks), whereas ESR normalizes much more slowly (3–4 weeks).

optionExplanations.A: A 2-week course is dangerously inadequate and is associated with high rates of treatment failure, relapse, and development of chronic osteomyelitis.
optionExplanations.B: Two weeks of IV antibiotics without oral consolidation therapy provides insufficient total duration (<4–6 weeks) to sterilize infected cortical bone.
optionExplanations.C: Per the source key (the classic curriculum regimen), uncomplicated pediatric hematogenous osteomyelitis is treated with 3 weeks of IV antibiotics followed by 3 weeks of oral antibiotics; the source notes that modern guidelines allow earlier oral transition.
optionExplanations.D: Initial therapy must be intravenous to rapidly achieve high bactericidal serum and bone concentrations and overcome bacteremia.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall the classic treatment regimen for pediatric acute hematogenous osteomyelitis: initial intravenous antibiotic therapy followed by oral consolidation therapy to complete a 6-week curative course.

questions.question: A 20-year-old college student sustains a closed, displaced spiral midshaft fracture of the right humerus following a fall from an electric scooter. On physical examination in the trauma bay, the patient is unable to actively extend his right wrist, metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, or thumb, demonstrating a pronounced wrist drop. He also has loss of sensation over the dorsal first web space of the hand. Radial and ulnar pulses are 2+ and symmetric. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.E: Axillary nerve

questions.explanation:
The radial nerve is the most commonly injured peripheral nerve in skeletal trauma, complicated by humeral shaft fractures in 10% to 18% of cases. Anatomically, the radial nerve travels within the spiral (radial) groove on the posterior aspect of the middle third of the humerus, resting directly against the periosteum before piercing the lateral intermuscular septum. Fractures of the humeral midshaft (especially spiral fractures or distal-third oblique fractures—the Holstein-Lewis fracture) place the radial nerve at extreme risk of stretching, contusion, entrapment, or laceration. Radial nerve palsy produces the classic clinical picture: 1. Wrist drop: Inability to actively extend the wrist (denervation of extensor carpi radialis longus/brevis). 2. Inability to extend fingers and thumb: Loss of extensor digitorum communis and extensor pollicis longus. 3. Sensory loss: Numbness over the dorsal first web space (superficial radial nerve). In closed fractures, >85–90% of radial nerve palsies are neurapraxias that recover spontaneously within 3 to 4 months of observation.

High-yield clinical pearl: HOLSTEIN-LEWIS FRACTURE:
A spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft where the radial nerve is particularly tethered as it pierces the lateral intermuscular septum, carrying an especially high risk of entrapment.

Exam trap: Do not perform immediate nerve exploration in a closed humeral shaft fracture with primary radial nerve palsy! Manage with functional bracing (Sarmiento brace); >85% resolve spontaneously. Surgery is indicated if the palsy develops *after* closed reduction (secondary entrapment) or in open fractures.

optionExplanations.A: Wrist drop with loss of sensation over the dorsal first web space after a humeral shaft fracture indicates radial nerve injury in the spiral groove.
optionExplanations.B: Ulnar nerve injury causes claw hand deformity (4th/5th digits), loss of interosseous abduction/adduction, and sensory loss over the hypothenar and volar 5th digit.
optionExplanations.C: Median nerve injury impairs thumb opposition (thenar wasting), flexor pollicis longus/FDP of index finger, producing the 'Benediction sign' or 'ape hand'.
optionExplanations.D: Musculocutaneous nerve innervates biceps brachii, coracobrachialis, and brachialis; injury impairs elbow flexion and causes sensory loss over lateral forearm (LABCN).
optionExplanations.E: Axillary nerve injury occurs in surgical neck humerus fractures and anterior shoulder dislocations, causing deltoid paralysis and loss of sensation over the 'regimental badge' lateral shoulder.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that midshaft humeral fractures injure the radial nerve in the spiral groove, manifesting clinically as wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space.

questions.question: A 32-year-old motorcycle driver is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed collision. He has an obvious open fracture of the right tibia with an active 4-cm wound communicating with the fracture site and visible bone ends. The patient is hemodynamically stable. Which of the following statements represents the correct initial management step for this open fracture?

options.A: Grade III fractures are treated with a first-generation cephalosporin alone
options.B: Early bone stabilization worsens soft tissue healing and should be postponed whenever possible
options.C: Antibiotics should be delayed until operative cultures are obtained in the operating room
options.D: Wounds should be assessed, gently irrigated with sterile saline, dressed sterilely, and IV antibiotics should be given immediately on admission
options.E: Severely contaminated fractures should be reduced in the emergency room to remove debris early

questions.explanation:
Open fractures are true orthopedic emergencies requiring a strict, standardized treatment sequence to minimize infection and osteomyelitis: 1. Immediate Intravenous Antibiotics: Systemic IV antibiotics are the single most critical factor in reducing open fracture infection rates and must be administered immediately on admission (ideally within 1 hour). Delaying antibiotics >3 hours significantly increases the risk of deep infection. 2. Wound Assessment & Sterile Dressing: In the emergency room, gross superficial contamination is gently removed, the wound is photographed for documentation, covered with a sterile saline-soaked gauze dressing, and splinted. The wound should NOT be repeatedly uncovered or probed in the ER to prevent hospital-acquired nosocomial superinfection. 3. Formal Operative Debridement: Emergent surgical formal irrigation and debridement is performed in the sterile operating room, followed by skeletal stabilization (external fixation or intramedullary nailing).

High-yield clinical pearl: GUSTILO-ANDERSON CLASSIFICATION & ANTIBIOTIC COVERAGE:
• TYPE I:
Clean wound < 1 cm -> 1st gen Cephalosporin (Cefazolin).
• TYPE II:
Wound 1–10 cm without extensive soft tissue damage -> Cefazolin.
• TYPE III:
High energy, wound > 10 cm, extensive crushing/contamination -> Cefazolin + Aminoglycoside (Gentamicin).
• SOIL / BARNYARD CONTAMINATION:
Add High-Dose Penicillin (covers Clostridium perfringens).

Exam trap: The single most important intervention in the ER that decreases infection in open fractures is the TIMING OF SYSTEMIC INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS (<1–3 hours from injury).

optionExplanations.A: Grade III open fractures require broad-spectrum coverage: a first-generation cephalosporin (Cefazolin) PLUS an aminoglycoside (Gentamicin) or third-generation cephalosporin for Gram-negative bacilli; farmyard/soil contamination requires adding Penicillin/Ampicillin for Clostridium.
optionExplanations.B: Early rigid skeletal stabilization (external fixator or IM nail) promotes soft tissue healing, protects vascularity, and decreases infection rates.
optionExplanations.C: Antibiotics must NEVER be delayed for wound or operative cultures; ER wound cultures correlate poorly with true infecting organisms and delaying antibiotics causes disastrous infection rates.
optionExplanations.D: Initial open-fracture care is to assess the wound, gently irrigate and sterilely dress it, and give IV antibiotics immediately on admission, before formal operative debridement.
optionExplanations.E: Contaminated bone ends should NOT be aggressively reduced back into the soft tissue envelope in the ER before formal operative debridement, as doing so drags contaminated debris deep into uninfected tissue planes.

questions.educationalObjective: State the correct emergency protocol for open fractures: immediate intravenous antibiotic administration, sterile saline dressing, splint stabilization, and prompt transfer to the operating room for formal surgical debridement.

questions.question: A 78-year-old unmarried woman underwent successful open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) for a displaced femoral neck fracture 4 days ago. She is medically stable, taking oral medications for type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Prior to the fall, she lived completely alone in a third-floor apartment in an older building with no elevator. She currently requires moderate assistance to transfer, ambulates short distances using a rolling walker, and finds navigating stairs extremely difficult and painful. She has no surviving children, relatives, or local family support. What is the most appropriate next intervention for this patient?

options.A: None of your business as a doctor
options.C: Move her to seniors home permanently
options.E: Keep her in the same ER-busy hospital

questions.explanation:
Discharge planning and comprehensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation are vital core components of geriatric hip fracture management (orthogeriatric care). This elderly patient lives alone in a third-floor walk-up apartment with no elevator and has no family caregivers. Because she cannot safely navigate stairs or perform independent activities of daily living (ADLs) with her walker, discharging her directly home would place her at extreme risk of immediate falls, severe neglect, and mortality. However, permanent placement in a nursing home is premature and inappropriate, as she was independently functional prior to her acute hip fracture. The correct, standard-of-care intervention is transfer to an inpatient rehabilitation hospital or skilled nursing subacute rehabilitation facility. Inpatient rehabilitation provides daily physical and occupational therapy, progressive weight-bearing, gait re-training, and stair negotiation until she can regain sufficient functional independence to safely return to community living.

High-yield clinical pearl: ORTHOGERIATRIC CARE GOALS:
Early mobilization within 24 hours of hip fracture surgery, aggressive multimodal analgesia (femoral/PENG nerve blocks), delirium prevention, osteoporosis medical treatment (bisphosphonates/calcium/vitamin D), and structured step-down inpatient rehabilitation.

Exam trap: Always match the patient's discharge destination to their physical environment and social support. A patient who cannot climb stairs cannot go home to a walk-up apartment.

optionExplanations.A: Physicians bear direct ethical, clinical, and legal responsibility for ensuring a safe, medically sound discharge plan that prevents preventable readmissions and adverse outcomes.
optionExplanations.B: Discharging her to an unassisted 3rd-floor apartment without an elevator will lead to immediate fall recurrence and catastrophic re-injury.
optionExplanations.C: Permanent institutionalization in a senior nursing home strip the patient of independence before she has been given the opportunity to rehabilitate.
optionExplanations.D: She cannot yet manage stairs or live alone safely but was independent before the fracture, so transfer to an inpatient rehabilitation facility is the standard-of-care next step.
optionExplanations.E: Prolonged acute hospital admission in an acute inpatient bed increases risks of hospital-acquired nosocomial infections (C. difficile, MRSA), deep vein thrombosis, and delerium.

questions.educationalObjective: Select inpatient rehabilitation hospital transfer as the safest and most effective discharge disposition for an elderly hip fracture patient with environmental barriers and lack of home social support.

questions.question: A 35-year-old construction worker underwent plate and screw fixation for a Gustilo-Anderson Type IIIA open tibial shaft fracture 6 months ago. The surgical incision healed, but for the past 4 months, he has had a persistent draining sinus tract over the anteromedial shin with continuous seropurulent discharge. He has received multiple prolonged courses of oral and intravenous antibiotics with only transient reductions in drainage. Plain radiographs show mature fracture union, but there is lucency surrounding the cortical screws and a dense segment of detached necrotic cortex. Which of the following is the best management?

options.E: Oral antibiotics

questions.explanation:
This patient has chronic post-traumatic osteomyelitis with an infected hardware retention and a draining cutaneous sinus tract. Bacteria (particularly S. aureus and S. epidermidis) form an impenetrable glycocalyx biofilm on metallic orthopedic implants (plates, screws, intramedullary nails). Once a biofilm forms, bacteria become metabolically quiescent and resistant to concentrations of antibiotics up to a thousand times higher than minimum inhibitory concentrations; systemic antibiotics cannot sterilize colonized metallic hardware. Because the fracture has now successfully united (healed at 6 months), the metallic implant no longer serves a mechanical purpose and acts solely as a contaminated foreign body nidus for chronic infection. The definitive, mandatory treatment is implant/metal removal, radical surgical debridement of all infected soft tissues and necrotic bone (sequestrectomy), curettage of the sinus tract, and pathogen-directed postoperative antibiotics.

High-yield clinical pearl: MARJOLIN'S ULCER:
A rare but highly aggressive SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA arising within a longstanding, chronic draining sinus tract or burn scar of >20–30 years duration. Biopsy is indicated for any non-healing ulcer with nodular edges.

Exam trap: Do not remove hardware if the fracture is NOT yet united! If the fracture is still ununited, stable hardware must be preserved (or replaced with an external fixator) until union is achieved; once united, remove metal immediately.

optionExplanations.A: A united fracture with chronic implant-associated osteomyelitis and a draining sinus needs hardware removal and radical debridement, because antibiotics alone cannot clear biofilm on retained metal.
optionExplanations.B: IV antibiotics alone cannot penetrate or eradicate mature biofilm on metallic foreign bodies and will fail as long as the hardware remains in situ.
optionExplanations.C: Corticosteroids are immunosuppressive and strictly contraindicated in active osteomyelitis.
optionExplanations.D: Untreated chronic sinus tract drainage risks secondary malignant degeneration (Marjolin's ulcer—squamous cell carcinoma) and progressive bone loss.
optionExplanations.E: Long-term suppressive oral antibiotics are reserved only for ununited fractures where hardware cannot yet be removed or in patients medically unfit for surgery.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that once a fracture has healed, the definitive treatment for persistent hardware infection and draining sinus tracts is complete hardware removal and surgical debridement.

questions.question: A 45-year-old right-hand-dominant active carpenter sustains a high-energy fall onto his outstretched hand, resulting in a displaced, comminuted intra-articular fracture of the distal radius with a 3-mm articular step-off and dorsal comminution. Closed reduction and splinting are attempted in the emergency department, but post-reduction radiographs show recurrent dorsal displacement, radial shortening of 5 mm, and persistent 3-mm incongruity of the radiocarpal joint. What is the best definitive management for this patient?

options.E: Continued casting

questions.explanation:
Intra-articular fractures of the distal radius in young or active patients demand anatomical reduction and stable fixation to prevent post-traumatic radiocarpal osteoarthritis and severe functional disability. An intra-articular step-off greater than 1 to 2 mm, radial shortening >3 mm, or dorsal tilt >10° are established criteria for fracture instability and failure of non-operative management. When closed reduction fails to achieve or maintain acceptable alignment (recurrent displacement in cast), the gold-standard definitive treatment is open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with a volar locking plate. ORIF directly restores articular congruity under direct visualization, corrects radial length and inclination, and provides rigid biomechanical stability that permits early wrist mobilization, preventing post-traumatic stiffness.

High-yield clinical pearl: ACCEPTABLE RADIOGRAPHIC PARAMETERS FOR DISTAL RADIUS REDUCTION:
• Radial inclination: >15° (normal ~22°).
• Radial height/length: within 2–3 mm of contralateral side (normal ~11–12 mm).
• Volar tilt: neutral to 10° volar (normal ~11° volar tilt).
• Articular step-off: < 1 TO 2 MM (most critical parameter for preventing post-traumatic OA!).

Exam trap: In active patients, any intra-articular step-off >2 mm that cannot be reduced closed is an absolute indication for ORIF.

optionExplanations.A: Skeletal traction is an obsolete, temporary measure that cannot provide stable definitive articular reconstruction for distal radius fractures.
optionExplanations.B: Functional bracing cannot maintain reduction in an unstable intra-articular fracture with dorsal comminution.
optionExplanations.C: Observation guarantees catastrophic malunion with severe wrist pain, loss of grip strength, and rapid post-traumatic radiocarpal arthrosis.
optionExplanations.D: An unstable intra-articular distal radius fracture that redisplaces after closed reduction needs open reduction and internal fixation, typically with a volar locking plate.
optionExplanations.E: Continued casting has already failed; persistent immobilization will simply result in cast loosening, re-displacement, and complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS).

questions.educationalObjective: Identify failed closed reduction and persistent articular incongruity in a distal radius fracture as an absolute indication for open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF).

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy falls from the monkey bars onto his outstretched hand with the elbow in hyperextension. He presents to the emergency department with acute, massive elbow swelling, S-shaped arm deformity, ecchymosis over the antecubital fossa, and intense pain. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the elbow demonstrate a Gartland Type III completely displaced extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture with posterior displacement of the distal fragment. What is the most serious neurovascular complication that must be monitored and urgently evaluated in this patient?

options.E: Brachial artery injury

questions.explanation:
Supracondylar humerus fractures are the most common pediatric elbow fracture, peaking at ages 5 to 8 years. In extension-type fractures (>95% of cases), the distal humeral fragment displaces posteriorly, causing the sharp, jagged anterior spike of the proximal humeral metaphysis to thrust forward into the antecubital fossa. This directly impinges, kinks, tears, or causes severe spasm of the brachial artery and the median nerve (specifically its anterior interosseous nerve [AIN] branch). Brachial artery occlusion or compression precipitates acute anterior forearm compartment ischemia, leading to the devastating, irreversible condition known as Volkmann ischemic contracture (infarction of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus, followed by fibrous contracture and claw hand). Monitoring distal vascular status (radial pulse, capillary refill, skin color, and temperature) is the single most critical priority in emergency supracondylar fracture care.

High-yield clinical pearl: THE 'PINK PULSELESS HAND':
If the radial pulse is absent but the hand is warm, pink, with brisk capillary refill (<2 sec), it indicates collateral flow. The patient requires URGENT CLOSED REDUCTION AND PERCUTANEOUS PINNING (CRPP) in the operating room. In >80% of cases, reduction of the fracture relieves arterial kinking and the pulse returns.

Exam trap: Never flex the elbow beyond 90° in a displaced supracondylar fracture before surgical fixation! Extreme flexion obliterates collateral circulation and causes compartment syndrome.

optionExplanations.A: Avascular necrosis of the trochlea or capitellum is exceedingly rare in supracondylar fractures compared to lateral condyle fractures.
optionExplanations.B: Radial nerve palsy can occur with posteromedial displacement of the distal fragment, but is far less catastrophic than vascular limb ischemia from brachial artery injury.
optionExplanations.C: Supracondylar fractures in children are metaphyseal and have tremendous vascularity; nonunion or delayed union is virtually unheard of.
optionExplanations.D: Myositis ossificans can occur after aggressive passive elbow manipulation, but is not the most serious immediate limb-threatening emergency.
optionExplanations.E: In a displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture the anterior spike of the proximal fragment can injure the brachial artery, risking forearm ischemia and Volkmann contracture.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify brachial artery injury as the most serious, limb-threatening complication of pediatric displaced supracondylar humerus fractures, predisposing to Volkmann ischemic contracture.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy trips and falls while running on a school playground, landing on his outstretched right hand. He presents to the pediatric clinic with focal pain, swelling, and a mild angular deformity of the distal third of his forearm. Plain anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the forearm demonstrate a fracture line completely disrupting the tensile cortex on the convex side of the bone, while the compressive cortex on the opposite concave side remains intact and plastically deformed without cortical discontinuity. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Comminuted fracture

questions.explanation:
Pediatric bone has unique biomechanical properties compared to adult bone: it has higher collagen content, lower mineral density, higher porosity, and a remarkably thick, vascular periosteal sleeve. These characteristics allow pediatric bone to absorb tremendous plastic deformation and energy before breaking. A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture that occurs when an angular bending force exceeds the ultimate strength of the bone: 1. The convex surface fails under tensile stress, resulting in a cortical breach/fracture line. 2. The concave surface is loaded in compression and plastically bends without macroscopic cortical discontinuity, resembling the bending and snapping of a young, green tree twig. In contrast, a torus (buckle) fracture is caused by pure axial compression, producing an outward bulging or buckling of the cortex without any breach of cortical continuity.

High-yield clinical pearl: MANAGEMENT OF GREENSTICK FRACTURES:
Because the intact concave cortex remains under plastic deformation, it will act as an internal spring, causing the deformity to recur inside the cast if not addressed. The orthopedic surgeon must often complete the fracture on the concave side under sedation to achieve stable reduction before casting.

Exam trap: Do not confuse greenstick fracture (tension side broken, compression side bent) with torus/buckle fracture (compression side crumpled, no tension break).

optionExplanations.A: A torus (buckle) fracture involves outward wrinkling/buckling of the cortex under compression without any disruption or crack in either cortex.
optionExplanations.B: Spiral fractures represent complete cortical failure in a spiral trajectory resulting from torsional/twisting forces.
optionExplanations.C: Transverse fractures are complete bicortical fractures perpendicular to the long axis of the bone.
optionExplanations.D: A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture in which the convex (tensile) cortex breaks while the concave (compressive) cortex bends plastically and stays intact.
optionExplanations.E: Comminuted fractures have three or more complete fracture fragments, typical of high-energy adult trauma.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose a greenstick fracture as an incomplete pediatric fracture characterized by a cortical breach on the convex tension side with an intact, plastically deformed concave cortex.

questions.question: An orthopedic resident systematically evaluates the orthogonal anteroposterior (AP) and lateral forearm radiographs of a trauma patient with diaphyseal radius and ulna fractures (both bone forearm fracture), as displayed in the test examination sheet. The resident carefully inspects the displacement parameters— translation, angulation, rotation, and shortening. Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE regarding the deformity observed in the bones on this patient's radiographs?

options.A: In the lateral view there is no translation in ulnar fracture while there is minimal translation in the radius
options.B: From the X-rays we can judge that this patient is an adult with fully calcified physes
options.C: In the AP view ulnar fragments are overlapped
options.D: Apex of the angle seen in the AP view is towards lateral
options.E: No rotation of distal fragments of both radius and ulna in both views

questions.explanation:
Accurate radiographic analysis of long bone fractures requires assessing four fundamental parameters on orthogonal (AP and lateral) views: translation, angulation, rotation, and shortening. 1. Translation (shift or apposition): Describes the degree of sideways motion of the distal fracture fragment relative to the proximal fragment, expressed as a percentage of cortical contact. On the lateral radiographic projection of this patient, the ulnar fracture fragments demonstrate excellent cortical alignment with no translational displacement, whereas the radial fracture exhibits slight, minimal translation. This exact radiographic finding corresponds directly to Option A. 2. In both-bone forearm fractures (diaphyseal radius and ulna), anatomical reduction with restoration of the radial bow and interosseous space is paramount to preserve forearm pronation and supination.

High-yield clinical pearl: THE FOREARM AS A JOINT:
The radius and ulna function mechanically as a bicentric joint (superior and inferior radioulnar joints linked by the interosseous membrane). Even a 10° angular malunion of the radius can cause up to a 50% loss of forearm pronation and supination!

Exam trap: Always examine orthogonal views (AP and Lateral) together! A fracture that appears perfectly reduced on the AP view may be completely displaced or angulated on the lateral view.

optionExplanations.A: Per the source key, on the lateral view the ulnar fracture fragments keep cortical contact (0% translation) while the radius shows minimal translation. This depends on the radiograph, which is not reproduced in the PDF.
optionExplanations.B: Careful inspection of the distal radius and ulna in the examination image clearly reveals open, radiolucent epiphyseal growth plates (physes), indicating a pediatric/adolescent patient, not an adult.
optionExplanations.C: In the AP view, the ulnar fragments do not display significant overlapping or shortening; they are predominantly angulated.
optionExplanations.D: The apex of the deformity on the AP view is directed medially (toward the ulnar side), not laterally.
optionExplanations.E: Rotational deformity cannot be completely excluded and is typically present in displaced forearm fractures due to the unapposed pull of the pronator teres, supinator, and pronator quadratus.

questions.educationalObjective: Master the systematic radiographic evaluation of fractures, accurately describing displacement parameters (translation, angulation, rotation, shortening) on orthogonal projections.

questions.question: A 22-year-old male is brought to the trauma center by emergency medical services after a high-speed rollover vehicular crash. On arrival, he is in profound circulatory shock with a blood pressure of 75/40 mmHg. However, in stark contrast to typical trauma presentations, his pulse is 48 beats/min (bradycardia) rather than tachycardia. His skin is warm, flushed, and dry, and physical examination reveals flaccid paralysis and areflexia below the level of the T2 dermatome. Which of the following is the most likely type of shock?

options.E: Obstructive shock

questions.explanation:
This patient presents with pathognomonic features of neurogenic shock secondary to acute cervical or high thoracic spinal cord injury (typically at or above T6). Neurogenic shock is a subtype of distributive shock caused by the sudden disruption of descending sympathetic outflow from the brainstem and autonomic sympathetic chain. This produces a dual hemodynamic collapse: 1. Massive Arterial and Venous Vasodilation: Loss of vascular sympathetic tone causes pooling of blood in the peripheral venous capacitance beds, drastically reducing systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and cardiac preload, causing severe hypotension. The skin appears paradoxically warm, pink, and dry. 2. Paradoxical Bradycardia: Disruption of the cardiac accelerator sympathetic fibers (originating from T1–T4 spinal cord levels) leaves the heart subject to unapposed parasympathetic vagal tone, preventing the normal compensatory baroreceptor-mediated tachycardia. The combination of hypotension + bradycardia + warm extremities in a trauma patient is diagnostic of neurogenic shock. Management requires IV crystalloids followed by alpha-1 adrenergic vasopressors (norepinephrine or phenylephrine) to restore vascular tone.

High-yield clinical pearl: NEUROGENIC SHOCK VS SPINAL SHOCK:
• NEUROGENIC SHOCK:
A hemodynamic phenomenon (hypotension + bradycardia) due to loss of sympathetic vascular/cardiac tone from injury above T6.
• SPINAL SHOCK:
A neurologic phenomenon representing transient total loss of all spinal cord reflex and motor activity below the lesion (areflexia, flaccidity). The termination of spinal shock is signaled by the return of the BULBOSACRAL (BULBOCAVERNOSUS) REFLEX.

Exam trap: In any trauma patient in shock, assume HYPOVOLEMIC (HEMORRHAGIC) SHOCK FIRST until proven otherwise. However, when hypotension is accompanied by BRADYCARDIA AND WARM PERIPHERIES , identify NEUROGENIC SHOCK.

optionExplanations.A: Hypovolemic (hemorrhagic) shock is the most common shock in trauma; however, it is universally characterized by compensatory tachycardia (>100 bpm), cool, pale, clammy extremities, and delayed capillary refill.
optionExplanations.B: Cardiogenic shock (e.g., myocardial contusion) presents with hypotension, elevated jugular venous distension, pulmonary edema, and tachycardia with cold extremities.
optionExplanations.C: Septic shock presents with tachycardia, fever, leukocytosis, and warm flushed skin in late stages, but not acute post-traumatic bradycardia with areflexic paralysis.
optionExplanations.D: Hypotension with bradycardia, warm dry flushed skin and flaccid paralysis below the level of a high spinal injury indicates neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone.
optionExplanations.E: Obstructive shock (tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade) presents with severe hypotension, tachycardia, and jugular venous distension.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize neurogenic shock by its classic triad of severe hypotension, paradoxical bradycardia, and warm dry skin secondary to loss of sympathetic tone following acute cervical or high-thoracic spinal cord injury.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department after sustaining a high-energy closed comminuted tibial shaft fracture in a motorcycle collision. Over the next 4 hours, he develops escalating, intractable pain in his leg that is completely out of proportion to the injury and unresponsive to escalating doses of intravenous opioids. On physical examination, the anterior and lateral leg compartments are intensely tense, firm, and 'woody' on palpation. Mild passive plantarflexion and passive stretch of the toes elicits agonizing, screaming pain. He also complains of tingling and paresthesias in the first web space of the foot. Distal dorsalis pedis pulses are palpable but weak. What is the most appropriate emergency management?

options.A: Elevate the limb and reassess after 6 hours
options.E: Open reduction and internal fixation alone

questions.explanation:
This patient presents with textbook, classic acute compartment syndrome (ACS) of the leg following a high-energy tibial shaft fracture (the single most common injury associated with ACS). In ACS, post-traumatic hemorrhage and tissue edema increase interstitial pressure within a non-yielding osteofascial compartment. When intracompartmental pressure rises above capillary perfusion pressure (typically when the Delta pressure [Diastolic blood pressure minus Intracompartmental pressure] is < 30 mmHg), microvascular capillary blood flow ceases, leading to ischemic tissue necrosis of neuromuscular structures within 6 to 8 hours. The clinical hallmarks are: 1. Pain out of proportion to the underlying injury, refractory to narcotics (the earliest symptom). 2. Severe, excruciating pain on passive stretching of the muscles within the affected compartment (the most sensitive clinical sign). 3. Tense, woody, non-yielding compartment firmness. 4. Hypesthesia/paresthesia (deep peroneal nerve in 1st web space for anterior compartment). Acute compartment syndrome is a true limb-threatening surgical emergency. The mandatory, immediate treatment is emergent four-compartment fasciotomy of the leg (via dual medial and lateral incisions) to completely decompress all four compartments (anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, deep posterior).

High-yield clinical pearl: PULSELESSNESS IS A LATE SIGN:
The presence of a palpable distal pulse does NOT rule out compartment syndrome! Intracompartmental pressures (30– 45 mmHg) easily exceed capillary pressure (25–30 mmHg) to kill muscle while remaining well below systolic arterial pressure (120 mmHg). If pulses are absent, irreversible gangrene and necrosis have already occurred.

Exam trap: Never elevate the leg above the heart in suspected compartment syndrome! Keep the limb neutral at heart level, immediately remove all bivalve casts and tight dressings down to skin, and rush to the operating room for fasciotomy.

optionExplanations.A: Limb elevation is strictly contraindicated in compartment syndrome because elevating the leg reduces arterial perfusion pressure, exacerbating tissue ischemia; the leg should be kept level with the heart.
optionExplanations.B: Applying a cast or circumferential dressing further restricts tissue expansion, dramatically worsening compartment pressures.
optionExplanations.C: Observation and opioids will allow progressive muscle infarction and permanent ischemic contracture (Volkmann-like necrosis) or need for amputation.
optionExplanations.D: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense 'woody' compartments and paresthesias after a tibial shaft fracture indicate acute compartment syndrome, which needs emergency fasciotomy.
optionExplanations.E: ORIF stabilizes the bone but does not decompress the swollen soft tissue compartments; performing ORIF without full fasciotomy is fatal to limb viability.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify acute compartment syndrome by intractable pain out of proportion to injury and severe pain on passive stretch, and recognize emergent four-compartment fasciotomy as the mandatory definitive treatment.

questions.question: A 24-year-old previously healthy male is hospitalized following an acute closed, displaced femoral shaft fracture sustained in a high-speed motorcycle accident. Approximately 36 hours post-injury, while awaiting intramedullary nailing, he develops sudden tachypnea, tachycardia, progressive shortness of breath with hypoxemia (pulse oximetry 84% on ambient air), acute confusion, disorientation, and agitation. On physical examination, diffuse non-blanching petechiae are observed across his upper chest, anterior axillary folds, and subconjunctival spaces. Chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral diffuse patchy infiltrates ('snowstorm' pattern). Which of the following best explains the underlying pathophysiology of this patient's condition?

options.B: Circulating fat globules causing endothelial injury and inflammation
options.E: Microthrombi due to platelet aggregation alone

questions.explanation:
This clinical vignette depicts textbook Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES) occurring 24 to 72 hours after a long-bone (femoral/tibial) shaft fracture. FES is diagnosed clinically by Gurd's classic triad: 1. Respiratory insufficiency: Tachypnea, acute hypoxemia, dyspnea progressing to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). 2. Neurological impairment: Acute encephalopathy, confusion, restlessness, and delirium out of proportion to hypoxemia. 3. Petechial rash: Non-blanching petechiae over the chest, neck, axilla, and conjunctiva due to fat emboli microvascular occlusion and capillary fragility (present in 20–50% of patients and virtually pathognomonic). Pathophysiology involves a dual mechanism: • Mechanical: Disrupted medullary intramedullary fat droplets and bone marrow enter ruptured venous sinusoids at the fracture site, traveling to the pulmonary capillary bed. • Biochemical: Circulating fat globules are hydrolyzed by local pulmonary endothelial lipases into toxic free fatty acids (FFAs). These free fatty acids induce intense endothelial damage, acute capillary leakage, platelet activation, alveolar pneumocyte destruction, and systemic systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Prevention is achieved by early operative fixation and stabilization of the femoral fracture (within 24 hours); treatment is primarily supportive (supplemental oxygen, mechanical ventilation).

High-yield clinical pearl: PREVENTION OF FAT EMBOLISM:
EARLY DEFINITIVE STABILIZATION AND FIXATION OF LONG BONE FRACTURES (WITHIN 24 HOURS OF TRAUMA) dramatically reduces the incidence and severity of Fat Embolism Syndrome by stopping ongoing marrow extravasation at the fracture site.

Exam trap: Timing distinguishes FES from PE: FAT EMBOLISM OCCURS EARLY (24 TO 72 HOURS) and presents with a PETECHIAL RASH. VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM (PE) OCCURS LATER (>5 TO 7 DAYS) and lacks petechiae.

optionExplanations.A: Thromboembolic pulmonary embolism (PE) secondary to deep vein thrombosis (DVT) typically occurs 5 to 14 days post-injury, does NOT cause a petechial rash, and results from a dislodged venous fibrin clot, not fat globules.
optionExplanations.B: In fat embolism syndrome, marrow fat globules enter the circulation and are hydrolyzed to toxic free fatty acids that injure the endothelium and cause inflammation, producing hypoxemia, confusion and petechiae.
optionExplanations.C: Alveolar edema and hemorrhage are secondary manifestations of the acute lung injury, not the primary initiating cellular pathophysiology.
optionExplanations.D: Air embolism occurs following central venous catheter manipulation, decompression sickness, or cardiothoracic surgery, not delayed 36 hours after closed skeletal trauma.
optionExplanations.E: Platelet aggregation and microthrombi occur secondarily to endothelial injury induced by toxic free fatty acids, but the primary etiologic driver is circulating bone marrow fat globules.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain the pathophysiology of Fat Embolism Syndrome following long-bone fracture: marrow fat droplets enter the circulation and are metabolized into toxic free fatty acids that cause direct endothelial injury, capillary leak, and the classic triad of hypoxemia, confusion, and petechial rash.
